facts.title: LBV 1806-20 is a stellar heavyweight
facts.teaser: This luminous blue variable may hold about 165 solar masses—among the heaviest stars we know.

**LBV 1806-20** is a **luminous blue variable** hidden deep in the Milky Way. Its estimated **165 solar masses** place it on the short list of the most massive stars astronomers have catalogued.

facts.title: How thunderclouds charge up
facts.teaser: Colliding ice crystals and graupel separate charge—positive aloft, negative below—until lightning strikes.
facts.body_md:
Inside a **thundercloud**, rising **ice crystals** rub against heavier **graupel** pellets. The crystals tend to carry **positive** charge upward while graupel stays **negative** lower down—building the voltage that can discharge as **lightning**.

[Lightning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning)

facts.title: Fulminology means studying lightning
facts.teaser: From Latin fulmen ("thunderbolt"), the word labels the scientific study of lightning itself.
facts.body_md:
Scientists who study lightning work in **fulminology**, from Latin **fulmen** ("thunderbolt"). The related adjective **fulminous** once described anything sudden and thunderous—though today the field is mostly about physics and safety, not etymology alone.

[Lightning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning)

facts.title: One lightning bolt isn't "a billion volts simple
facts.teaser: A flash can release hundreds of megajoules, but peak voltage and current vary wildly strike to strike.
facts.body_md:
Pop science often quotes a single giant number for lightning's power. Real strikes span a wide range—often **hundreds of megajoules**—with **voltage and current** that depend on cloud height, path length, and return strokes. Treating every bolt as identical oversimplifies the physics.

[Lightning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning)

The 'stepped leader' of lightning establishes the channel over hundreds of milliseconds, while the actual discharge takes only a few dozen microseconds.

facts.title: Why lightning prefers stranded wire
facts.teaser: The skin effect keeps current on a conductor's surface—so multi-stranded cables handle surges better.
facts.body_md:
High-frequency current in a conductor hugs the outer surface—the **skin effect**. For **lightning protection**, multi-stranded or braided conductors offer more surface area than a solid rod of the same diameter, helping safely carry a strike.

[Lightning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning)

facts.title: Venus is hotter than Mercury at the surface
facts.teaser: Thick CO₂ clouds trap heat on Venus, pushing surface temperatures above 460°C—hotter than Mercury.
facts.body_md:
**Venus** orbits farther from the Sun than **Mercury**, yet its dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere creates a runaway greenhouse. Surface probes measured about **460°C**, making it the hottest planet in the Solar System.

[Venus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus)

facts.title: Siberia's coldest month on record
facts.teaser: In January 1892, Verkhoyansk averaged −56.7°C—the Northern Hemisphere's coldest monthly mean.
facts.body_md:
Verkhoyansk in eastern Siberia sits in a deep basin where cold, dense air can pool for weeks. Its **January 1892** monthly average of **−56.7°C** still stands among the most extreme sustained cold spells ever measured in the Northern Hemisphere.

[List of weather records (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_weather_records)

facts.title: Greenland logged −69.6°C in 1991
facts.teaser: On 22 December 1991, the Greenland Ice Sheet recorded −69.6°C—a Northern Hemisphere cold extreme.
facts.body_md:
Automatic weather stations on the Greenland Ice Sheet catch brief, brutal cold snaps. The **−69.6°C** reading on **22 December 1991** remains one of the lowest temperatures ever confirmed in the Northern Hemisphere—far below everyday winter chill in populated regions.

[List of weather records (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_weather_records)

facts.title: Montana's 57°C swing in one day
facts.teaser: In January 1972, Loma, Montana, warmed from −48°C to +9°C within 24 hours—a world record jump.
facts.body_md:
Automated stations caught an extreme **chinook** event in the Rockies. Thermometers at **Loma, Montana**, rose about **57°C** between morning and afternoon on **15 January 1972**—the largest 24-hour temperature change reliably measured.

[List of weather records (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_weather_records)

facts.title: The first newspaper weather forecast
facts.teaser: On 1 August 1861, The Times printed a public weather outlook—an act of humility about an uncertain science.
facts.body_md:
Forecasting once seemed almost audacious. When **Robert FitzRoy** published the first daily weather outlook in **The Times** in **1861**, readers got probabilities, not promises—a reminder that science often means sharing doubt honestly.

[Weather forecasting (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_forecasting)

facts.title: Dunkirk evacuation began in 1940
facts.teaser: On 26 May 1940, Operation Dynamo started—hundreds of small boats helped rescue Allied soldiers trapped in France.
facts.body_md:
After German forces cut off Allied armies in northern France, **Operation Dynamo** began on **26 May 1940**. Over nine days, naval ships and a flotilla of fishing boats and pleasure craft evacuated more than **338,000** soldiers from the beaches of **Dunkirk**.

[Dunkirk evacuation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkirk_evacuation)

facts.title: Who coined "ice age"?
facts.teaser: Botanist Karl Schimper used the term in 1837, but Louis Agassiz later downplayed his rival's role.
facts.body_md:
**Karl Friedrich Schimper** coined *Eiszeit* ("ice age") in **1837** and argued that glaciers had once covered much of Europe. **Louis Agassiz** popularized the idea but left Schimper out of key publications after a bitter personal feud.

[Ice age (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_age)

facts.title: A scrap of papyrus linked to Cleopatra
facts.teaser: Papyrus Bingen 45 may preserve one word in the queen's own handwriting—a rare trace of her script.
facts.body_md:
**Papyrus Bingen 45** is a tax receipt from **51 BCE**. Scholars debate whether a single word was written by **Cleopatra VII** herself or by a clerk—but if authentic, it would be one of the few surviving samples of her handwriting.

[Papyrus Bingen 45 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papyrus_Bingen_45)

facts.title: The Dead Sea sits far below sea level
facts.teaser: Its shoreline near Ein Bokek is about 430 m below global sea level—the lowest exposed land on Earth.
facts.body_md:
The **Dead Sea** lies in the Jordan Rift Valley, where tectonic plates pull apart. With no outlet, evaporation leaves hypersaline water; the shoreline near **Ein Bokek** sits roughly **430 m** below mean sea level—the lowest dry land on the planet.

[Dead Sea (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Sea)

facts.title: Venus flytraps count touches before snapping shut
facts.teaser: Two triggers within 0.5–30 seconds close the trap—filtering out raindrops and stray debris.
facts.body_md:
A **Venus flytrap** only slams shut after **two** hair triggers fire within about **0.5 to 30 seconds**. That simple timing filter lets the plant ignore single bumps from rain or litter while still catching live prey.

[Venus flytrap (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_flytrap)

facts.title: Octopuses have three hearts
facts.teaser: Two pump blood to the gills; one feeds the rest of the body—and it pauses when the animal swims.
facts.body_md:
An **octopus** circulates copper-rich, blue blood through **three hearts**. Two branchial hearts push blood through the gills; the systemic heart supplies the body. When an octopus swims, the systemic heart actually **stops**, which is one reason they prefer crawling.

[Octopus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octopus)

facts.title: Seattle pool opened a day late at 100°F
facts.teaser: A thermostat glitch heated Queen Anne Pool to 38°C in 1995, delaying its public opening by one day.
facts.body_md:
On the eve of its **1995** reopening, a faulty thermostat at **Queen Anne Pool** in Seattle drove the water to about **100°F (38°C)**. Crews cooled it overnight, so the neighborhood swim opened one day behind schedule.

[Queen Anne Pool (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Anne_Pool)

facts.title: Everest was summited on 29 May 1953
facts.teaser: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the top—news broke on the eve of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation.
facts.body_md:
On **29 May 1953**, **Edmund Hillary** and **Tenzing Norgay** stood on the summit of **Mount Everest**. The triumph became a global cultural moment—timed, by coincidence, just before the coronation of **Elizabeth II**.

[1953 British Mount Everest expedition (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_British_Mount_Everest_expedition)

facts.title: Umami joined the classic taste map
facts.teaser: Sweet, sour, salty, and bitter were long the quartet—umami (savory) is now recognized as a fifth basic taste.
facts.body_md:
For centuries Western textbooks listed **four** basic tastes. **Umami**, the savory depth in broth, cheese, and tomatoes, was identified by **Kikunae Ikeda** in **1908** and is now accepted as a fifth taste with its own receptors.

[Umami (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami)

facts.title: A 1919 eclipse tested Einstein's gravity
facts.teaser: Starlight bent near the Sun during totality—early proof that space itself curves around mass.
facts.body_md:
During the **29 May 1919** solar eclipse, **Arthur Eddington** photographed stars near the Sun's limb. Their apparent shift matched **Einstein's** prediction that gravity bends light—dramatic evidence for general relativity.

[Eddington experiment (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_experiment)

facts.title: A cow learned to scratch with a brush
facts.teaser: In 2024, researchers filmed a cow using a stiff brush as a tool—the first documented case in cattle.
facts.body_md:
Farm animals are smarter than barnyard stereotypes suggest. In **2024**, scientists recorded a **cow** picking up a stiff brush to scratch an itchy spot—one of the first clear cases of **tool use** documented in cattle.

[Tool use by animals (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tool_use_by_animals)

facts.title: Chori uses six contrastive tones
facts.teaser: Spoken in Nigeria, Chori is among the world's most tone-rich languages—pitch can change word meaning six ways.
facts.body_md:
In **Chori**, spoken in **Nigeria**, pitch is not decoration—it carries meaning. Linguists have documented **six** contrastive tone levels, among the richest tone systems known in any language.

[Tone (linguistics) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tone_(linguistics))

facts.title: Joan of Arc was executed on 30 May 1431
facts.teaser: Her trial for heresy raised enduring questions about conscience, authority, and when law outruns justice.
facts.body_md:
**Joan of Arc** was burned at the stake in **Rouen** on **30 May 1431** after a politically charged heresy trial. Philosophers and historians still debate how states should weigh **individual conscience** against official authority.

[Joan of Arc (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc)

facts.title: World No Tobacco Day
facts.teaser: Every 31 May, WHO spotlights tobacco's health and economic toll—and policies that help people quit.
facts.body_md:
Since **1988**, the **World Health Organization** has marked **31 May** as **World No Tobacco Day**. Campaigns highlight addiction, second-hand smoke, and the social costs of an industry that still kills millions each year.

[World No Tobacco Day (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_No_Tobacco_Day)

facts.title: First U.S. copyright law signed in 1790
facts.teaser: On 31 May 1790, President Washington approved a statute balancing authors' rights with public learning.
facts.body_md:
The **Copyright Act of 1790**, signed on **31 May**, gave American authors **14-year** terms (renewable once). It aimed to encourage books and maps while still allowing ideas to enter the public domain—an early template for intellectual-property law.

[Copyright Act of 1790 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_Act_of_1790)

facts.title: Johnstown Flood reshaped U.S. insurance
facts.teaser: On 31 May 1889, a dam break killed more than 2,200 people—one of the costliest disasters of the 19th century.
facts.body_md:
After heavy rain, the **South Fork Dam** failed on **31 May 1889**, sending a wall of water through **Johnstown, Pennsylvania**. More than **2,200** people died. The staggering losses pushed insurers and lawmakers to rethink **disaster risk** and liability.

[Johnstown flood (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnstown_flood)

facts.teaser: Surface temperatures range from about 35°C down to −143°C—average near −63°C on the Red Planet.
facts.body_md:
Thin air and distance from the Sun make **Mars** thermally wild. Near the equator, summer afternoons can approach **35°C**, while polar winter nights plunge near **−143°C**; the global average is about **−63°C**.

[Mars (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars)

facts.title: Why Linked Lists Still Matter
facts.teaser: Arrays win at random access, but linked lists dominate when you need fast inserts and deletes.
facts.body_md:
In a **linked list**, each element points to the next, so inserting or removing a node takes **O(1)** time — you just rewire a couple of pointers. The tradeoff is that finding the *n*-th element requires walking the chain from the start, making random access **O(n)**.

This is the mirror image of arrays, where reading any index is instant but inserting in the middle means shifting every subsequent element. Modern CPUs favour arrays because of cache locality, yet linked lists remain essential inside **operating system schedulers**, memory allocators, and undo-history stacks where constant-time splicing matters more than sequential reads.

[Linked list (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linked_list)

facts.title: Zero was invented, not discovered
facts.teaser: The concept of zero as a number took centuries to be accepted.

[More on zero (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/0)

facts.title: Elephants are the only animals that can't jump
facts.teaser: Despite their strength, elephants physically cannot jump.
facts.body_md:
Elephants are the **only known mammals** that cannot jump. Their leg bones are all pointed downward, meaning they don't have the "spring" structure that other animals use to push off the ground. Despite this, they can move at speeds up to **40 km/h** in a running walk.

[More on elephants (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elephant)

facts.title: Neutron Stars in Science Fiction
facts.teaser: Sci-fi authors have imagined life on, around, and even inside neutron stars despite their extreme conditions.
facts.body_md:
Neutron stars pack the mass of the Sun into a sphere roughly **20 km** across, with surface gravity about **200 billion** times Earth's. Despite these lethal conditions, science fiction has imagined creatures that thrive there.

In Robert Forward's *Dragon's Egg* (1980), tiny intelligent beings called **cheela** live on a neutron star's surface, experiencing time a million times faster than humans. Stephen Baxter's *Flux* places organisms inside a star's superfluid interior. These stories let authors explore how radically different physics could still produce life.

[Neutron stars in fiction (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutron_stars_in_fiction)

facts.title: Why Git Uses SHA-1 Hashes
facts.teaser: Git hashes every commit with SHA-1 — not for security, but to guarantee your code never silently changes.
facts.body_md:
When Linus Torvalds designed Git in 2005, he chose **SHA-1** to fingerprint every object — blobs, trees, commits, and tags. The goal was **data integrity**, not cryptographic security: if even one bit flips in storage or transit, the hash won't match and Git will notice.

Torvalds himself put it simply: *"You can trust that five years later, you get the exact same data you put in."* After the 2017 SHAttered collision attack, Git began transitioning to **SHA-256**, but the original design philosophy remains — hashes are content addresses, not trust anchors.

[Git (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Git)

facts.title: The NSA once withdrew its own hash standard
facts.teaser: SHA-0 was published in 1993, then quietly replaced a year later.
facts.body_md:
The hash function now called **SHA-0** was published by NIST in **1993** as a US federal standard. Less than two years later it was replaced by **SHA-1** after the NSA made a technical revision that was never fully explained in public. That unusual retreat made SHA-0 a small but famous dead end in cryptography history.

[SHA-0 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-1#SHA-0)

facts.title: When Browsers Banned SHA-1 Certificates
facts.teaser: In 2017 every major browser stopped trusting SHA-1 SSL certificates after researchers proved the hash could be forged.
facts.body_md:
For years, security experts warned that **SHA-1** was too weak for SSL/TLS certificates, but migration was slow. The tipping point came in February 2017 when Google and CWI Amsterdam published the **SHAttered** attack — the first practical SHA-1 collision, producing two different PDFs with the same hash.

Within weeks, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari all **rejected SHA-1 certificates** by default. Certificate authorities had already been issuing SHA-256 replacements, but SHAttered turned a theoretical risk into a demonstrated exploit, forcing the last holdouts to upgrade overnight.

[SHA-1 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-1)

facts.title: Old cryptography can outlive old software
facts.teaser: Dropping SHA-1 support forced vendors to reconsider how long trust policies should last.
facts.body_md:
When Microsoft ended **SHA-1** code signing support for Windows Update, it showed that security decisions are not only technical but also **policy decisions**. Software vendors, certificate authorities, and regulators all have to decide how long old cryptographic systems remain acceptable. In practice, trust on the internet is governed by rules as much as by math.

[Code signing (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_signing)

facts.title: Breaking SHA-1 Now Costs Just $45,000
facts.teaser: A chosen-prefix collision attack on SHA-1 can be rented in the cloud for about $45,000 — well within reach of criminals.
facts.body_md:
In 2020, researchers demonstrated a **chosen-prefix collision** against SHA-1 using rented GPU time on the cloud. The total cost: roughly **$45,000** and a few weeks of computation.

A chosen-prefix attack is far more dangerous than a simple collision because the attacker controls the beginning of both files, making it practical to forge certificates or sign malicious code. At $45,000, the attack is affordable for **organized crime groups** and intelligence agencies — but still too expensive for casual hackers. The result cemented SHA-1's status as cryptographically broken for any security-critical use.

[SHA-1 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-1)

facts.title: PlayStation 3s That Broke HTTPS
facts.teaser: In 2008 researchers used a cluster of PlayStation 3 consoles to forge a trusted web certificate by exploiting MD5 weaknesses.
facts.body_md:
At the 25th Chaos Communication Congress in 2008, a team of researchers revealed they had used **200 PlayStation 3 consoles** to generate an MD5 collision. The result was a **rogue Certificate Authority certificate** that browsers trusted completely.

With that forged CA, the team could mint valid HTTPS certificates for *any* website — enabling undetectable man-in-the-middle attacks. They chose PS3s because the Cell processor's SPUs were exceptionally fast at the parallel math needed for collision-finding. The demo prompted certificate authorities worldwide to **abandon MD5** and switch to SHA-based signatures.

[MD5 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MD5)

facts.title: The Roman Slave Collar With a Bounty
facts.teaser: The Zoninus collar is the only known Roman slave collar that promises a reward for returning the wearer.
facts.body_md:
Discovered in Rome, the **Zoninus collar** is a bronze ring inscribed in Latin: *"Hold me, lest I flee, and return me to my master Zoninus — you will receive a gold coin."* It is the only known Roman slave collar that offers a **cash reward** for the wearer's return.

Such collars were riveted around the necks of enslaved people considered flight risks. Most bore only the owner's name and a plea to detain. The Zoninus collar's added bounty suggests its owner either had an especially determined runaway — or placed an unusually high value on that particular person.

[Zoninus collar (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoninus_collar)

facts.title: The MD5 Hash Hidden in a Military Logo
facts.teaser: US Cyber Command embedded an MD5 hash of its mission statement in its official emblem as a nerdy Easter egg.
facts.body_md:
When **US Cyber Command** unveiled its emblem in 2009, observers noticed a ring of 32 hexadecimal characters around the inner gold seal. It turned out to be the **MD5 hash** of the command's mission statement.

The hash — `9ec4c12949a4f31474f299058ce2b22a` — was a deliberate design choice, a cryptographic wink aimed at the tech-savvy community USCYBERCOM serves. It also became an unintentional commentary on the weakness of MD5 itself: anyone with the mission text could verify the hash in seconds, making it a **fingerprint**, not a secret.

[United States Cyber Command (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cyber_Command)

facts.title: Corkscrew Plants: Underground Predators
facts.teaser: Genlisea plants use twisted underground leaves to trap and digest soil organisms — no snapping required.
facts.body_md:
The genus **Genlisea**, known as corkscrew plants, has developed one of the most unusual carnivorous strategies in the plant kingdom. Instead of flashy traps above ground, they hunt **underground** with modified leaves shaped like a Y.

Each arm of the Y spirals into a corkscrew lined with **inward-pointing hairs**. Microscopic organisms like protists and nematodes can enter but cannot back out — the hairs act as one-way turnstiles, funnelling prey toward a digestive chamber at the junction. Some Genlisea species also hold the record for the **smallest known plant genomes**, with as few as 63 million base pairs.

[Genlisea (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genlisea)

facts.title: Crocodiles Can't Stick Out Their Tongue
facts.teaser: A crocodile's tongue is fused to the floor of its mouth, so it can never stick it out or use it to catch food.
facts.body_md:
Unlike most reptiles, a **crocodile's tongue** is almost completely attached to the roof and floor of its mouth by a membrane. This means it cannot protrude, move food around, or lick its lips.

So how does a crocodile eat? It relies on powerful jaws and a **"death roll"** to tear prey into swallowable chunks, then tilts its head back and lets gravity do the rest. The fixed tongue does serve one purpose: a special valve called the **palatal valve** at the back of the throat seals off the airway, allowing the crocodile to open its mouth underwater without drowning.

[Crocodile (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile)

facts.title: The first email was sent in 1971
facts.teaser: Ray Tomlinson sent the first network email and chose the @ symbol for addresses.
facts.body_md:
Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between two computers on ARPANET in **1971**. He chose the **@ symbol** to separate the user name from the computer name — a convention that persists in every email address today. Tomlinson later said the content of that first message was something like "QWERTYUIOP."

[More on email history (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Email)

facts.title: The British Network That Beat ARPANET
facts.teaser: Britain's NPL network implemented packet switching in early 1969 — months before ARPANET sent its first message.
facts.body_md:
Most people credit ARPANET as the first packet-switched network, but the **NPL network** at Britain's National Physical Laboratory got there first. Built by Donald Davies and his team, it began operating in early **1969**, months before ARPANET's famous "LO" message in October.

Davies independently coined the term **"packet switching"** — a concept also developed by Paul Baran at RAND. The NPL network ran at **768 kbit/s**, far faster than ARPANET's initial 50 kbit/s lines. Though it remained a local research network rather than a cross-country system, its design influenced ARPANET's own protocol choices.

[NPL network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPL_network)

facts.title: How Umami Became the Fifth Taste
facts.teaser: In 1908 a Japanese chemist extracted glutamate from seaweed broth and proved a fifth basic taste existed.
facts.body_md:
For centuries Western science recognized only four basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, and bitter. In 1908, Japanese chemist **Kikunae Ikeda** challenged that model. He noticed that dashi broth made from **kombu seaweed** had a savoury depth that none of the four could explain.

Ikeda isolated the molecule responsible — **glutamic acid** — and named the taste *umami*, roughly meaning "pleasant savoury taste." Western scientists remained sceptical for nearly a century, until **2002** when researchers identified dedicated umami receptors on the human tongue, finally confirming it as a legitimate fifth basic taste.

[Umami (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami)

facts.title: The Great Wall of China is not visible from space
facts.teaser: Despite the popular myth, astronauts cannot see the Great Wall from orbit.
facts.body_md:
Contrary to popular belief, the **Great Wall of China** is **not visible from low Earth orbit** with the naked eye. Multiple astronauts, including Yang Liwei (China's first astronaut), have confirmed this. The wall is narrow (about 5-8 meters wide) and blends with the surrounding landscape.

[More on the Great Wall (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China)

facts.title: Goethe's Heartbreak Became a Masterpiece
facts.teaser: Goethe channelled his unrequited love into The Sorrows of Young Werther — an early example of sublimation.
facts.body_md:
In the early 1770s, young Johann Wolfgang von **Goethe** fell deeply for Charlotte Buff, who was engaged to another man. Rather than collapse under the pain, he poured it into his 1774 novel *The Sorrows of Young Werther*.

The book became a sensation across Europe and is often cited as a textbook case of **sublimation** — the psychological defence mechanism where unacceptable emotions are redirected into socially valued activities. Goethe later said the novel saved his life by externalizing feelings he could not resolve. Ironically, the book triggered a wave of copycat suicides across Europe, a phenomenon now called the **Werther effect**.

[The Sorrows of Young Werther (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sorrows_of_Young_Werther)

facts.title: One Script, Many Languages
facts.teaser: Chinese characters were adopted to write Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, and dozens of other unrelated languages.
facts.body_md:
**Chinese characters** (hanzi) originated over 3,000 years ago for a single language, yet they spread across East Asia to write languages with completely different grammars and phonologies. Japanese uses them as **kanji** alongside two native syllabaries; Korean employed them as **hanja** for centuries before Hangul became dominant; and Vietnamese used a modified set called **chữ Nôm** until the Latin-based quốc ngữ replaced it.

The appeal was cultural prestige and the ability to convey meaning across language barriers — a Chinese and Japanese reader could grasp the same character even if they pronounced it differently. Today, only Chinese and Japanese still use the characters in everyday writing.

[Chinese characters (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_characters)

facts.title: TCP/IP and the Birth of 'Internet
facts.teaser: Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published the TCP/IP design in 1974 — and that December, the word "internet" appeared for the first time.
facts.body_md:
In May 1974, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published *"A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication"*, describing a system that would let incompatible networks talk to each other. The core idea was a **two-layer design**: TCP handled reliable delivery while IP handled routing across networks.

That December, **RFC 675** used the word "internet" — short for *internetwork* — for the first time in an official document. The concept was revolutionary: instead of building one giant network, you could stitch together thousands of independent ones. By 1983, ARPANET switched fully to TCP/IP, and the modern Internet was born.

[Internet protocol suite (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_protocol_suite)

facts.title: ARPANET's Tiny Four-Node Start
facts.teaser: By December 1969 ARPANET connected just four universities in the western US — the seed of today's global Internet.
facts.body_md:
The network that became the Internet started with just **four nodes** by the end of 1969: UCLA, Stanford Research Institute, UC Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah. All were in the **western United States**, connected by 50 kbit/s leased telephone lines.

The very first message, sent on October 29 from UCLA to Stanford, was supposed to be "LOGIN" — but the system **crashed after "LO."** The full connection was restored an hour later. Within a year, ARPANET expanded to 13 nodes, and by the mid-1970s it linked sites across the country, proving that packet switching could work at scale.

[ARPANET (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARPANET)

facts.title: Tardigrades can survive in outer space
facts.teaser: These microscopic animals endure extreme radiation, vacuum, and temperatures.
facts.body_md:
Tardigrades (water bears) are microscopic animals that can survive **extreme conditions**: temperatures from −272°C to 150°C, pressures 6 times greater than the deepest ocean, and **radiation** hundreds of times above lethal human doses. In 2007, they became the first animals to **survive exposure to outer space.**

[More on tardigrades (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tardigrade)

facts.title: Turing's Proof That Some Problems Can't Be Solved
facts.teaser: In 1936 Alan Turing proved that no algorithm can determine whether an arbitrary program will halt — a foundational limit of computation.
facts.body_md:
Alan Turing's 1936 paper *"On Computable Numbers"* introduced the concept of a **Turing machine** — an abstract device that formalizes what it means to compute. Using it, he proved the **halting problem**: there is no general algorithm that can decide, for every possible program and input, whether that program will eventually stop or run forever.

This was more than a curiosity. The halting problem established a hard boundary on what computers can do, no matter how powerful. It also showed that Hilbert's *Entscheidungsproblem* — the dream of a mechanical procedure to decide all mathematical truths — was **impossible**.

[Halting problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halting_problem)

facts.title: Chaitin's Omega is a number you can define but never compute
facts.teaser: Gregory Chaitin defined a halting probability Ω that encodes which programs halt — a perfectly well-defined real number that no algorithm can ever fully calculate.
facts.body_md:
In 1975, Gregory Chaitin defined the halting probability **Ω** — a real number between 0 and 1 that represents the probability that a randomly chosen program will eventually stop running. Each bit of Ω encodes the answer to an independent halting question.

What makes Ω remarkable is that it's **algorithmically random**: no pattern or shortcut exists for computing its digits. You can approximate it from below, but every new digit requires solving an entirely new undecidable problem. It's the mathematical embodiment of irreducible complexity.

[Chaitin's constant (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaitin%27s_constant)

facts.title: First dogs in space survived a 100 km flight in 1951
facts.teaser: Dezik and Tsygan became the first dogs to reach space and return alive, launched on a Soviet R-1 rocket in July 1951.
facts.body_md:
On 22 July 1951, two stray dogs named **Dezik** and **Tsygan** were launched aboard a Soviet R-1 rocket from the Kapustin Yar range. They reached an altitude of about 100 km — crossing the Kármán line into space — and returned safely by parachute.

The flight lasted only minutes, but it proved that living creatures could survive the forces of launch and brief weightlessness. Tsygan was later adopted by physicist Anatoli Blagonravov. Dezik flew again just a week later on a second mission, but tragically did not survive when the parachute failed.

[Dezik and Tsygan (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dezik_and_Tsygan)

facts.title: Rice's theorem makes all program behavior undecidable
facts.teaser: Rice's theorem proves that no algorithm can decide any non-trivial property about the behavior of arbitrary programs.
facts.body_md:
Published by Henry Gordon Rice in 1953, this theorem dramatically extends the halting problem. It states that for **any** non-trivial property of the function computed by a program — whether it produces output, whether it's equivalent to another program, whether it ever enters a certain state — no general algorithm can decide it.

A property is "non-trivial" if it's true for some programs and false for others. The only decidable properties are the trivial ones: those true for all programs or none. This means all interesting questions about program behavior are fundamentally unanswerable in general.

[Rice's theorem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice%27s_theorem)

facts.title: The term "halting problem" appeared 16 years after the proof
facts.teaser: Martin Davis first used the phrase "halting problem" in 1952, even though Turing's original undecidability proof dates back to 1936.
facts.body_md:
Alan Turing proved in **1936** that no general procedure can determine whether an arbitrary program will terminate. But he never called it the "halting problem" — his paper discussed the *Entscheidungsproblem* and "circular" versus "circle-free" machines.

It took until **1952** for mathematician Martin Davis to coin the now-famous term in his book *Computability and Unsolvability*. The catchy name helped transform an abstract logical result into one of computer science's most recognizable concepts, widely taught in every theory of computation course.

[Halting problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halting_problem)

facts.title: Binary choices explode faster than intuition
facts.teaser: A million on/off parts already create more states than you could ever list.
facts.body_md:
A system with **one million binary components** has \(2^{1,000,000}\) possible states. Written in decimal, that number has a bit over **300,000 digits**. Facts like this are a good reminder that exponential growth quickly outruns everyday intuition — even when the rule itself looks simple.

[Power of two (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_of_two)

facts.title: McCulloch-Pitts neurons launched computational neuroscience
facts.teaser: In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published the first mathematical model of a neuron, proving that networks of simple logic units could compute anything.
facts.body_md:
The **1943** paper "A Logical Calculus of Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity" showed that neurons could be modeled as binary threshold units. McCulloch was a neurophysiologist and Pitts a self-taught mathematical prodigy — he was just 20 years old.

Their key insight: a sufficiently large network of these idealized neurons can compute any function a Turing machine can. This was the first paper to bridge logic, computation, and brain science, directly inspiring both artificial intelligence and the later development of artificial neural networks.

[Artificial neuron (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_neuron)

facts.title: SNARC was the first neural network machine, built by a 24-year-old
facts.teaser: In 1951, Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC — the first hardware neural network — using 3,000 vacuum tubes and a surplus autopilot mechanism.
facts.body_md:
The Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator (**SNARC**) simulated 40 neurons using 3,000 vacuum tubes and the mechanical clutch system from a B-24 bomber's autopilot. Minsky was just a 24-year-old graduate student at Princeton when he built it.

SNARC learned by reinforcement: it modeled a virtual rat navigating a maze, strengthening connections when the rat moved toward the exit. The machine actually worked — the simulated rat learned to solve the maze. It was decades ahead of its time, but vacuum tube technology made it impractical to scale.

[Stochastic neural analog reinforcement calculator (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_neural_analog_reinforcement_calculator)

facts.title: Strachey's 1951 checkers program could beat casual players
facts.teaser: Christopher Strachey wrote one of the first game-playing programs in 1951 — a checkers AI running on the Ferranti Mark 1 that could complete full games.
facts.body_md:
In the summer of **1951**, Christopher Strachey wrote a draughts (checkers) program for the Ferranti Mark 1 at Manchester University. The program used the machine's entire memory — about 1,000 words — and could play a complete legal game from start to finish.

Strachey was not employed at the university; he was a schoolteacher who spent his holiday writing the program. He brought it in on a Friday evening and had it running by Monday. Alan Turing himself was so impressed that he gave Strachey access to the machine. It was one of the earliest demonstrations that computers could handle complex strategic reasoning.

[Christopher Strachey (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Strachey)

facts.title: Korean silk paintings found in a New Hampshire attic
facts.teaser: The earliest surviving silk-scroll paintings from Korea's Gangwon Province were discovered in an attic in Hopkinton, New Hampshire.
facts.body_md:
A set of rare **Buddhist silk paintings** from the Sinheungsa temple in Gangwon Province, South Korea, turned up thousands of miles from home — in an attic in the small town of Hopkinton, New Hampshire. They are believed to date from the Joseon Dynasty.

How they got there remains unclear, but they likely left Korea during the Japanese occupation or the Korean War. The paintings are significant because very few silk-scroll works from Gangwon Province survive, making this accidental discovery an important find for Korean art history.

[Sinheungsa (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinheungsa)

facts.title: The Turing Test checks for conversation, not intelligence
facts.teaser: Alan Turing proposed in 1950 that if a machine can converse indistinguishably from a human, it's reasonable to say it "thinks" — sidestepping the question of what intelligence really is.
facts.body_md:
In his 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," Turing replaced the question "Can machines think?" with a practical experiment: a human judge converses with both a machine and a human via text. If the judge can't reliably tell them apart, the machine passes.

Turing called it the **Imitation Game**, not the "Turing Test" — that name came later. He predicted that by the year 2000, machines would fool 30% of judges after five minutes of conversation. What he didn't anticipate was that modern chatbots would pass this bar while still lacking common sense, reigniting debates about whether the test measures intelligence or merely linguistic mimicry.

[Turing test (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_test)

facts.title: Trees trade nutrients through a fungal internet underground
facts.teaser: In 1997, Suzanne Simard proved that trees share carbon and nutrients through underground mycorrhizal fungal networks — dubbed the "Wood Wide Web.
facts.body_md:
Suzanne Simard's landmark **1997** experiment used radioactive carbon isotopes to demonstrate that paper birch and Douglas fir trees were actively exchanging carbon through shared **mycorrhizal fungi** in the soil. The fungi connect root systems of different trees, forming a vast underground network.

Through these networks, older "mother trees" can funnel sugars to shaded seedlings, and stressed trees can receive resources from healthier neighbors. The system even carries chemical warning signals about insect attacks. A single fungal network can connect dozens of trees across species boundaries, challenging the view of forests as collections of competing individuals.

[Mycorrhizal network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycorrhizal_network)

facts.title: Chimp fingerprints can fool human forensic experts
facts.teaser: Chimpanzee fingerprints are so similar to human ones that forensic examiners have difficulty telling them apart under a microscope.
facts.body_md:
Chimpanzees share roughly **98.7%** of our DNA, and their fingerprints reflect this closeness. They have the same loop, whorl, and arch patterns humans do, with similar ridge density and minutiae points — the very features forensic experts use for identification.

In practice, only subtle statistical differences in ridge spacing distinguish the two. This similarity has been cited in forensic literature as a potential source of misidentification at crime scenes near primate habitats. Koalas are the only other non-primate mammals known to have fingerprints convergently similar to ours.

[Chimpanzee (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimpanzee)

facts.title: The first computer mouse was made of wood
facts.teaser: Doug Engelbart built the first mouse prototype from wood in 1964.
facts.body_md:
Doug Engelbart invented the **computer mouse** in **1964** at the Stanford Research Institute. The first prototype was a **wooden shell** with two metal wheels inside. It was called a "mouse" because the cord coming out the back looked like a tail. Engelbart demonstrated it publicly in 1968 in what became known as the **"Mother of All Demos."**

[More on the computer mouse (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_mouse)

facts.title: AI hype is older than modern AI
facts.teaser: In 1965 Herbert Simon predicted machines would soon do most human work.
facts.body_md:
In **1965**, Herbert Simon predicted that within twenty years machines would be able to do **any work a human can do**. The quote is a classic example of how AI progress repeatedly inspires bold forecasts that outrun reality. It now reads less like engineering and more like a cultural artifact from the early age of computing optimism.

[Herbert A. Simon (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_A._Simon)

facts.title: Umami means "pleasant savory taste" in Japanese
facts.teaser: The word "umami" combines Japanese "umai" (delicious) with "mi" (taste) — a fifth basic taste not officially recognized by science until 2002.
facts.body_md:
Chemist Kikunae Ikeda coined the term **umami** in 1908 after isolating glutamate from kombu seaweed broth. He combined "umai" (うまい, delicious) with "mi" (味, taste) to describe the savory depth that didn't fit sweet, sour, salty, or bitter categories.

Despite Ikeda's discovery, Western science resisted accepting umami as a basic taste for nearly a century. It wasn't until **2002** that researchers identified specific tongue receptors (mGluR4) for glutamate, finally granting umami official status as the fifth fundamental taste alongside the traditional four.

[Umami (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami)

facts.title: Backpropagation existed for decades before AI noticed it
facts.teaser: The algorithm that powers modern deep learning was reinvented multiple times in control theory and statistics before AI researchers adopted it in the 1980s.
facts.body_md:
Backpropagation — the method of computing gradients through a neural network to update its weights — was first derived in **1960** by Henry J. Kelley for optimal control problems. Seppo Linnainmaa formalized automatic differentiation in 1970, and Paul Werbos applied it to neural networks in his 1974 PhD thesis.

Yet the AI community remained unaware until **1986**, when David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams published their famous paper demonstrating backprop's power for learning internal representations. That decade-long gap between invention and adoption cost neural network research years of progress — the technique might have prevented the first "AI winter" entirely.

[Backpropagation (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backpropagation)

facts.title: Blocks World was AI's favorite toy problem for a decade
facts.teaser: MIT's "Blocks World" — AI programs stacking colored blocks on a table — dominated artificial intelligence research in the 1960s-70s as a simplified model of reality.
facts.body_md:
In **Blocks World**, a program reasons about a table with colored blocks that can be stacked, moved, and rearranged. Terry Winograd's SHRDLU (1970) was the most famous system: you could type "Put the red block on top of the blue one" and it would plan and execute the moves.

The paradigm was seductive because it was tractable — a closed world with clear rules and no ambiguity. But this simplicity was also its downfall. Critics like Hubert Dreyfus argued that real intelligence doesn't work in neat, predefined domains. By the late 1970s, the AI community acknowledged that Blocks World success didn't transfer to the messy, open-ended real world.

[Blocks world (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blocks_world)

facts.title: Braille proves writing is spatial, not visual
facts.teaser: Braille demonstrates that the same linguistic principles work whether perceived by sight or touch — writing is fundamentally about spatial patterns, not vision.
facts.body_md:
Louis Braille published his system in **1829**, encoding the French alphabet into patterns of 1–6 raised dots within a 2×3 cell. Readers perceive these patterns through fingertips rather than eyes, yet they achieve reading speeds of 100–200 words per minute — comparable to sighted reading of print.

This challenges the assumption that writing is inherently visual. Braille shows that what matters is **spatial contrast** — distinct patterns arranged in sequence. The same principle underlies all writing systems: distinguishable marks in a consistent spatial framework. Whether those marks are ink on paper or bumps on a page, the linguistic function is identical.

[Braille (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braille)

facts.title: Rust guarantees memory safety without garbage collection
facts.teaser: Rust was designed to eliminate the memory corruption bugs that plague C and C++ — achieving safety through its ownership system rather than a runtime garbage collector.
facts.body_md:
Graydon Hoare started Rust as a personal project at Mozilla in **2006**, frustrated by memory bugs in Firefox's C++ codebase. The language's key innovation is its **ownership system**: every value has exactly one owner, and the compiler enforces borrowing rules at compile time, catching use-after-free, data races, and null pointer bugs before the code ever runs.

This "zero-cost abstraction" approach means Rust programs run as fast as C/C++ without sacrificing safety. By 2023, Rust code was being accepted into the Linux kernel — a milestone that took 30 years for any language besides C to achieve.

[Rust (programming language) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_(programming_language))

facts.title: Lake Baikal holds 20% of the world's fresh water
facts.teaser: This Siberian lake is the deepest and oldest on Earth.
facts.body_md:
Lake Baikal in **Siberia** is the **deepest lake** in the world (1,642 m) and the **oldest** (25-30 million years). It contains roughly **20% of the world's unfrozen surface fresh water** — more than all the North American Great Lakes combined.

[More on Lake Baikal (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal)

facts.title: The Dunning-Kruger effect works both ways
facts.teaser: People with low ability overestimate themselves, while experts underestimate theirs.
facts.body_md:
The **Dunning-Kruger effect** (1999) shows that people with **low competence** in a skill tend to greatly **overestimate** their ability, while **experts** tend to **underestimate** theirs. This happens because beginners lack the metacognitive skills to recognize their own mistakes.

[More on Dunning-Kruger (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunning%E2%80%93Kruger_effect)

facts.title: The US dollar bill costs 7.7 cents to print
facts.teaser: Producing physical currency costs far less than its face value.
facts.body_md:
It costs the US Bureau of Engraving and Printing about **7.7 cents** to produce a single one-dollar bill. The bill lasts about **6.6 years** in circulation before being replaced. Meanwhile, producing a **penny** costs about **2.7 cents** — making it cost more to produce than it's worth.

[More on US currency (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar)

facts.title: TypeScript took JavaScript from scripting to enterprise scale
facts.teaser: Microsoft created TypeScript in 2012 to add optional static typing to JavaScript — it's now used by over 80% of large-scale web projects.
facts.body_md:
Anders Hejlsberg — the same engineer behind C# and Turbo Pascal — led TypeScript's design at Microsoft. The insight was simple: don't replace JavaScript, just add an optional **type layer** that compiles away, catching bugs before runtime while remaining fully compatible with existing JS code.

By 2024, TypeScript had become the **4th most-used language** on GitHub. Its type system is unusually powerful — it's actually Turing-complete, meaning you can encode arbitrary computations in the type checker alone. This makes it both a pragmatic development tool and an accidental proof that type systems can be as expressive as programming languages themselves.

[TypeScript (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TypeScript)

facts.title: Anti-gravity for space travel appeared in fiction in 1827
facts.teaser: George Tucker's 1827 novel "A Voyage to the Moon" is the first known fiction to use anti-gravity as a means of space travel.
facts.body_md:
Published anonymously in **1827** by University of Virginia professor George Tucker, *A Voyage to the Moon* introduced a fictional metal called "lunarium" that repels Earth's gravity. The protagonist coats his spacecraft with it and floats to the Moon — no rockets needed.

This predates Jules Verne's *From the Earth to the Moon* (1865) by nearly four decades and H.G. Wells' gravity-blocking "cavorite" in *The First Men in the Moon* (1901) by over 70 years. Tucker's novel marks the transition from magical or divine space travel in literature to pseudo-scientific explanations — an early step toward hard science fiction.

[A Voyage to the Moon (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Voyage_to_the_Moon_(Tucker_novel))

facts.title: Go was designed to make programming boring again
facts.teaser: Ken Thompson and Rob Pike created Go at Google to fight complexity — intentionally leaving out features like inheritance and generics (initially) to keep the language simple.
facts.body_md:
Go emerged in **2009** from frustration with slow C++ compile times at Google. Its creators — **Ken Thompson** (co-creator of Unix, UTF-8, and B language) and **Rob Pike** (Plan 9, UTF-8) — deliberately designed it to be boring: no classes, no inheritance, no exceptions, minimal syntax.

The language's killer feature is built-in **concurrency** through goroutines — lightweight threads that cost just a few kilobytes of memory each. A single Go program can easily run millions of concurrent goroutines. This made it the default language for cloud infrastructure: Docker, Kubernetes, and Terraform are all written in Go.

[Go (programming language) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_(programming_language))

facts.title: Fertilizer production consumes 2% of all global energy
facts.teaser: The Haber-Bosch process for fixing nitrogen into fertilizer uses about 2% of the world's total energy output — quantum computing might eventually make it more efficient.
facts.body_md:
The **Haber-Bosch process** converts atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) into ammonia (NH₃) at extreme temperatures (400–500°C) and pressures (150–300 atm). It feeds roughly half the world's population, but the energy cost is staggering — about **2%** of global energy consumption each year.

Nature does the same job at room temperature: nitrogenase enzymes in soil bacteria fix nitrogen effortlessly. But the enzyme's mechanism involves quantum effects that are impossibly complex to simulate on classical computers. Quantum computers might eventually model nitrogenase precisely enough to inspire a room-temperature industrial catalyst — potentially saving 1% of all humanity's energy use.

[Haber process (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haber_process)

facts.title: Shor showed why quantum math matters
facts.teaser: A 1994 algorithm turned quantum computing from theory into a threat to RSA.
facts.body_md:
In **1994**, Peter Shor described a quantum algorithm for factoring large numbers much faster than known classical methods. That result gave quantum computing a concrete mathematical use-case with huge consequences for cryptography, especially **RSA**. It is one of the clearest examples of abstract math reshaping technology strategy.

[Shor's algorithm (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shor%27s_algorithm)

facts.title: China's Jiuzhang solved in seconds what would take 600M years
facts.teaser: The Jiuzhang photonic quantum computer performed a boson sampling calculation in 200 seconds that would take classical supercomputers 600 million years.
facts.body_md:
In December **2020**, a team led by Pan Jianwei at the University of Science and Technology of China demonstrated **Jiuzhang** — a photonic quantum computer that used 76 detected photons to perform Gaussian boson sampling. The calculation took about 200 seconds.

The fastest classical supercomputer would need an estimated **600 million years** for the same task. Unlike Google's Sycamore (which used superconducting qubits at near absolute zero), Jiuzhang operates at room temperature using light particles. It was the first quantum advantage demonstration that didn't rely on superconducting technology, proving that multiple hardware approaches can achieve quantum supremacy.

[Jiuzhang (quantum computer) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiuzhang_(quantum_computer))

facts.title: Helium-3 is a science bottleneck
facts.teaser: A rare isotope can become a real cost barrier for frontier labs.
facts.body_md:
**Helium-3** is not just an exotic gas for physics experiments. Because it is rare, expensive, and needed in specialized cryogenic systems, it can become a real **budget constraint** for advanced laboratories. In cutting-edge research, access to materials is often as important as access to ideas.

[Helium-3 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helium-3)

facts.title: Quantum theory became a computing blueprint
facts.teaser: The quantum Turing machine turned weird physics into an information model.
facts.body_md:
Paul Benioff's early work on the **quantum Turing machine** helped translate quantum mechanics into the language of computation. That mattered because it offered engineers and theorists a way to think about quantum systems as information-processing devices, not only as physics experiments. It became part of the conceptual bridge from theory to quantum hardware.

[Quantum Turing machine (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_Turing_machine)

facts.title: Martha Washington on US Paper Money
facts.teaser: She is the only woman ever featured on US paper currency — on an 1896 silver certificate.
facts.body_md:
Martha Washington's portrait appeared on the **1896 US one-dollar silver certificate**, making her the only woman ever depicted on American paper money. The certificate was part of the famous "Educational Series," prized by collectors for its elaborate allegorical artwork.

The Treasury chose her likeness partly to honor the role of First Ladies, yet **no woman has appeared on US paper currency since**. Efforts to feature women on bills — such as Harriet Tubman on the $20 — have been proposed but repeatedly delayed.

[History Instructing Youth (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_Instructing_Youth)

facts.title: RSA Was Secretly Invented at GCHQ
facts.teaser: Clifford Cocks devised the algorithm in 1973 — four years before Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman published theirs.
facts.body_md:
British mathematician Clifford Cocks invented what we now call RSA encryption while working at **GCHQ in 1973**, four years before Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman independently published their version at MIT. Because Cocks' work was classified, he received no public credit for decades.

The British discovery remained a state secret until **1997**, when GCHQ finally declassified the documents. By then, the "RSA" name was firmly established and the MIT trio had already commercialized the technology.

[RSA (cryptosystem) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem))

facts.title: Plants Pay Fungi With Carbon
facts.teaser: Trees send up to 30% of the carbon they fix through photosynthesis to fungal partners underground.
facts.body_md:
Plants can channel up to **30% of the carbon** they produce through photosynthesis to mycorrhizal fungi living on their roots. In return, these fungal networks supply the plants with nitrogen and phosphorus that would otherwise be inaccessible.

This underground exchange is not one-sided charity — it functions more like a **biological marketplace** where both partners adjust their contributions based on supply and demand. The fungal threads can extend meters beyond the root zone, vastly expanding a plant's effective reach.

[Mycorrhizal network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycorrhizal_network)

facts.title: Cat Purrs Can Heal Bones
facts.teaser: A cat's purr vibrates at 25–150 Hz — a frequency range known to promote bone density and tissue repair.
facts.body_md:
A domestic cat's purr oscillates between **25 and 150 Hz**, a range that biomedical research has linked to increased bone density and accelerated healing of fractures, tendons, and wounds. This may explain why cats recover from surgeries and falls remarkably quickly compared to dogs.

Cats purr not only when content but also when injured or stressed, suggesting the vibration serves a **self-healing function**. Some researchers believe this is why cats have fewer bone and joint problems despite spending much of their lives sleeping.

[Purr (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purr)

facts.title: Wi-Fi was invented in Australia
facts.teaser: The key patent behind Wi-Fi was developed by CSIRO in Australia.
facts.body_md:
The core technology behind **Wi-Fi** was developed in the **1990s** by John O'Sullivan and his team at **CSIRO** (Australia's national science agency). The invention grew out of research into detecting exploding mini black holes. CSIRO's patent became one of the most valuable ever filed by a research institution, earning over **$430 million** in licensing fees.

[More on Wi-Fi history (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi)

facts.title: Shakespeare invented over 1,700 English words
facts.teaser: Words like "lonely," "generous," and "eyeball" were coined by Shakespeare.
facts.body_md:
William Shakespeare is credited with **inventing over 1,700 words** in the English language, including "lonely," "generous," "eyeball," "bedroom," and "assassination." He also coined famous phrases like **"break the ice"** and **"wild goose chase."**

[More on Shakespeare's influence (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare%27s_influence)

facts.title: Umami Receptors Found in the Gut
facts.teaser: Scientists discovered umami taste receptors on the tongue in 2000 and then in the stomach in 2006.
facts.body_md:
Umami receptors were first identified on the human tongue in **2000**, confirming what Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda had proposed nearly a century earlier — that savory was a distinct fifth taste. Six years later, researchers found the same receptors in the **stomach lining**, suggesting the gut can "taste" amino acids directly.

The stomach receptors appear to trigger digestive responses when they detect glutamate, helping the body prepare for protein-rich food before it even reaches the intestines.

[Umami (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami)

facts.title: Cracking an 829-Bit RSA Key
facts.teaser: In 2020, researchers factored an 829-bit RSA key — it took the equivalent of 2,700 CPU-years of computation.
facts.body_md:
In 2020, a team of mathematicians successfully factored an **829-bit RSA key** (RSA-250), a feat requiring the equivalent of **2,700 CPU-years** of computation spread across a large cluster of machines. The effort used the General Number Field Sieve algorithm.

To put this in perspective, the widely used **RSA-2048** standard is estimated to need roughly a billion times more computational effort to crack — a gap that keeps current encryption safe, at least until quantum computers mature.

[RSA numbers (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_numbers)

facts.title: RSA became public because a patent expired
facts.teaser: The algorithm's legal status changed overnight in 2000.
facts.body_md:
RSA was covered by a US patent from **1983** until **September 2000**. Once that patent expired, the algorithm became much easier to use freely in software and standards. The math stayed the same, but its practical adoption changed because a legal barrier disappeared.

[RSA (cryptosystem) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem))

facts.title: Every Language Has Nouns and Verbs
facts.teaser: The distinction between nouns and verbs is one of the few true universals found in all known human languages.
facts.body_md:
Linguists have studied thousands of languages and found very few features shared by every single one. The existence of **nouns** (words for things) and **verbs** (words for actions or states) is among the most robust universals ever documented.

Even languages with radically different grammar — such as Mohawk, which builds entire sentences into single words — maintain this fundamental distinction. Some researchers argue it reflects a deep cognitive split between **objects and events** in human perception.

[Linguistic universal (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_universal)

facts.title: 512-Bit RSA Cracked on a Desktop
facts.teaser: A 512-bit RSA key can now be factored on a single desktop PC in about 73 days — in 1999 it needed hundreds of machines.
facts.body_md:
A **512-bit RSA key** can now be factored on a single desktop computer in roughly **73 days**. When the same key length was first broken in 1999 (RSA-155), it required a coordinated effort across hundreds of machines and the equivalent of 8,400 MIPS-years.

The dramatic speedup comes from both faster hardware and improved algorithms. This is why security standards have long since moved to **2048-bit and 4096-bit keys** — 512-bit RSA is considered completely broken for any serious use.

[RSA (cryptosystem) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem))

facts.title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
facts.teaser: Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate but only 225 to orbit the Sun.
facts.body_md:
Venus rotates so slowly that one **Venusian day** (one full rotation) takes **243 Earth days**, while its **orbital period** (one year) is only **225 Earth days**. This means a day on Venus is longer than its year. Additionally, Venus rotates **backwards** compared to most planets.

[More on Venus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus)

facts.title: Unix Began as a Pun on Multics
facts.teaser: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie created Unix at Bell Labs in 1969 — named 'Unics' as a joke on the bloated Multics system.
facts.body_md:
Unix was born at **Bell Labs in 1969** when Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie began building a small, clean operating system after their employer pulled out of the ambitious Multics project. They originally called it **"Unics"** — a pun on Multics, implying it did one thing well rather than trying to do everything.

The name was later respelled as "Unix." Thompson wrote the first version in assembly language for a spare **PDP-7** minicomputer, and the project grew largely because management didn't notice it was happening.

[Unix (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix)

facts.title: Honey never spoils
facts.teaser: Archaeologists found 3,000-year-old honey in Egyptian tombs that was still edible.
facts.body_md:
Honey is one of the only foods that **never spoils**. Archaeologists have found pots of honey in **Egyptian tombs** over 3,000 years old that were still perfectly edible. Honey's longevity comes from its low moisture content, high acidity, and natural production of **hydrogen peroxide.**

[More on honey (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honey)

facts.title: Unix changed computing by changing language
facts.teaser: Rewriting Unix in C turned an operating system into a portable model.
facts.body_md:
When Unix was rewritten in **C** in **1973**, it became far easier to move between different machines. That step helped turn Unix from one Bell Labs project into a historical template for modern operating systems. Portability became one of its most influential ideas.

[Unix (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix)

facts.title: Three Black Holes Colliding at Once
facts.teaser: Astronomers found a system where three supermassive black holes from merging galaxies are spiraling toward each other.
facts.body_md:
In the constellation Cancer, roughly **1.06 billion light-years** away, astronomers discovered **SDSS J0849+1114** — a system where three galaxies are merging and their supermassive black holes are spiraling toward one another.

Triple black hole mergers are extremely rare. This system is one of the tightest such configurations ever observed, with all three nuclei separated by less than **10,000 light-years**. The eventual merger will produce gravitational waves far more complex than those from binary black hole collisions.

[SDSS J0849+1114 (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SDSS_J0849%2B1114)

facts.title: Unix Dominated Supercomputing
facts.teaser: By the late 1990s, Unix and Unix-like systems powered over 90% of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers.
facts.body_md:
By the late 1990s, **Unix and Unix-like systems** ran on over **90%** of the machines on the TOP500 list of the world's fastest supercomputers. The combination of portability, networking, and multi-user design made Unix the natural choice for high-performance computing.

Today that dominance continues under the **Linux** banner — a Unix-like system that took over the TOP500 entirely. Since November 2017, every single supercomputer on the list runs Linux, including the current fastest machines exceeding **one exaflop** of performance.

[Unix (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix)

facts.title: Unix Licensed to Universities for $150
facts.teaser: The first Unix source-code license cost universities just $150, fueling its rapid spread through academia.
facts.body_md:
When AT&T began licensing Unix source code in the early 1970s, universities could obtain a copy for just **$150**. The low price — essentially a media and handling fee — made Unix accessible to computer science departments worldwide.

This bargain-priced access created an entire generation of programmers fluent in Unix. The **University of California, Berkeley** became a major hub, eventually producing **BSD** (Berkeley Software Distribution), which spawned its own family of operating systems still used today, including FreeBSD and parts of macOS.

[Unix (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix)

facts.title: Lost Unix V4 Tape Found in 2026
facts.teaser: A magnetic tape containing Unix Version 4 from 1973 was discovered at the University of Utah and successfully recovered.
facts.body_md:
In **2026**, a magnetic tape containing **Unix Version 4** (1973) was found at the University of Utah and its contents were successfully recovered. It is the earliest known surviving distribution of this version.

Before this discovery, Unix V4 was thought to be entirely lost — no source code or binaries had been preserved. The find gave historians their first direct look at the transitional version where Unix was being **rewritten from assembly into C**, a pivotal moment in computing history.

[Unix (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix)

facts.title: Do One Thing Well — The Unix Way
facts.teaser: The Unix philosophy of small, composable programs connected by pipes changed how all software is designed.
facts.body_md:
The **Unix philosophy** — write programs that do one thing well, and connect them using pipes — emerged from Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie's work at Bell Labs in the early 1970s. It was a radical departure from the monolithic software designs of the era.

This idea that complex behavior should arise from **combining simple tools** rather than building one giant program influenced everything from the Linux command line to modern microservices architecture and the API-driven web. Doug McIlroy, who invented Unix pipes, summarized it: *"Write programs that do one thing and do it well."*

[Unix philosophy (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_philosophy)

facts.title: Deep Blue Beat the World Chess Champion
facts.teaser: In 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov 3½–2½, becoming the first computer to beat a reigning champion.
facts.body_md:
On May 11, **1997**, IBM's **Deep Blue** defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov **3½–2½** in a six-game match in New York City. It was the first time a computer beat a reigning world champion under standard tournament conditions.

Deep Blue could evaluate **200 million positions per second** thanks to custom chess chips, but it was Kasparov's psychological unraveling — particularly after a mysterious move in Game 1 — that many analysts credit for the outcome. The match became a cultural milestone in the debate over human versus machine intelligence.

[Deep Blue (chess computer) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Blue_(chess_computer))

facts.title: Lightning is five times hotter than the Sun's surface
facts.teaser: A lightning bolt reaches 30,000°C — much hotter than the Sun's 5,500°C surface.
facts.body_md:
A **lightning bolt** can reach temperatures of about **30,000 Kelvin** (roughly 30,000°C) — about **five times hotter** than the surface of the Sun (5,500°C). Despite this extreme heat, a lightning strike is incredibly brief, lasting only about 1-2 microseconds per stroke.

[More on lightning (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning)

facts.title: Welsh Universities Led on Women's Access
facts.teaser: In 1900, 38% of Welsh university students were women — far ahead of most countries at the time.
facts.body_md:
By **1900**, women made up **38% of university students** in Wales, a remarkably high proportion for the era. This was partly because the University of Wales had admitted women from its founding in **1893**, unlike Oxford and Cambridge which restricted full degrees for women until 1920 and 1948 respectively.

Wales' progressive stance was driven by a strong nonconformist culture that valued education for all, and by the fact that Welsh universities were newer and less bound by centuries of tradition. The figure would not be matched by England until decades later.

[History of education in Wales (1870–1939) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_education_in_Wales_(1870%E2%80%931939))

facts.title: A Bug Made Deep Blue Look Brilliant
facts.teaser: A software bug caused Deep Blue to make a random move in Game 1, which Kasparov misread as superior intelligence.
facts.body_md:
During the first game of the **1997 rematch**, a bug in Deep Blue's evaluation code caused it to select a move essentially at random when it couldn't decide between options. Kasparov, stunned by the unexpected move, interpreted it as a sign of **deep strategic insight**.

The psychological impact was enormous. Kasparov later said the move haunted him throughout the match, contributing to his collapse in the decisive **Game 6**, which he resigned after just 19 moves. IBM's team only revealed the bug's role years later.

[Deep Blue (chess computer) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Blue_(chess_computer))

facts.title: Trees Warn Each Other Through Fungi
facts.teaser: Douglas firs attacked by insects send chemical alarm signals through underground fungal networks to neighboring pines.
facts.body_md:
When Douglas fir trees are attacked by insects, they can transmit **chemical warning signals** through mycorrhizal fungal networks to neighboring ponderosa pines. The recipient trees then ramp up production of **defense enzymes** before the insects even reach them.

This underground communication system — sometimes called the **"Wood Wide Web"** — demonstrates that forests are not collections of competing individuals but interconnected communities. The fungal threads linking the trees can span dozens of meters, creating a biological information network beneath the soil.

[Mycorrhizal network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycorrhizal_network)

facts.title: Newborn Pandas Are Shockingly Tiny
facts.teaser: A newborn giant panda weighs about 100 grams — roughly 1/900th of its mother's weight.
facts.body_md:
A newborn giant panda weighs just **90–130 grams** (about 3–4 ounces), making it one of the smallest mammalian newborns relative to its mother's size — roughly **1/900th** of the adult female's body weight. By comparison, a human newborn is about 1/20th of its mother's weight.

The tiny size is thought to result from the panda's low-energy **bamboo diet**, which cannot support the metabolic demands of growing a larger fetus. The cubs are born blind, hairless, and nearly helpless, requiring constant warmth from the mother for the first few weeks.

[Giant panda (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_panda)

facts.title: Bluetooth is named after a Viking king
facts.teaser: The Bluetooth standard was named after the 10th-century Danish king Harald Bluetooth.
facts.body_md:
The **Bluetooth** wireless standard was named after **Harald Bluetooth** (Harald Blåtand), a 10th-century king of Denmark who united dissonant Danish tribes. The idea was that Bluetooth technology would similarly unite different communication protocols. The Bluetooth **logo** is a combination of the runic initials H and B (ᚼ and ᛒ).

[More on Bluetooth (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluetooth)

facts.title: Why IBM Renamed Deep Thought to Deep Blue
facts.teaser: IBM changed the name from 'Deep Thought' to 'Deep Blue' because it sounded too much like the adult film 'Deep Throat.
facts.body_md:
IBM's chess computer was originally called **"Deep Thought"**, after the fictional computer in *The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy*. However, IBM's marketing department realized the name too closely resembled **"Deep Throat"** — both the Watergate informant and the notorious 1972 film.

The machine was renamed **"Deep Blue"**, combining "deep" (referencing the depth of its search algorithm) with "Big Blue" (IBM's longtime nickname). The rebranding proved fortunate — "Deep Blue" became one of the most recognized names in computing history.

[Deep Blue (chess computer) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Blue_(chess_computer))

facts.title: Umami Synergy — More Than the Sum
facts.teaser: Combining glutamate-rich foods with nucleotide-rich ones creates umami intensity far greater than either alone.
facts.body_md:
When foods rich in **glutamate** (like Parmesan cheese or tomatoes) are combined with those containing **nucleotides** like IMP or GMP (found in dried bonito or shiitake mushrooms), the perceived umami intensity can be **up to eight times stronger** than the sum of the individual ingredients.

This synergistic effect explains why classic flavor combinations work so well — Japanese dashi combines kombu (glutamate) with bonito flakes (IMP), and Italian cuisine pairs tomatoes with Parmesan. Chefs have exploited this principle for centuries, long before science identified the mechanism.

[Umami (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami)

facts.title: IBM Dismantled Deep Blue After Winning
facts.teaser: After beating Kasparov, IBM dismantled Deep Blue and refused a rematch — the prize was $700,000 for IBM.
facts.body_md:
After Deep Blue's historic victory over Kasparov in **1997**, IBM immediately **retired and dismantled** the machine, refusing Kasparov's repeated demands for a rematch. The match prize was **$700,000 for IBM** and $400,000 for Kasparov.

IBM's decision was strategic — they had achieved their publicity goal and feared a rematch loss would erase the gain. Kasparov accused IBM of cheating, claiming human grandmasters had intervened during games. IBM denied the allegations but never allowed independent verification, fueling conspiracy theories that persist to this day.

[Deep Blue (chess computer) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Blue_(chess_computer))

facts.title: Kasparov's Shifting View of Deep Blue
facts.teaser: Kasparov first called Deep Blue an 'alien opponent' but later dismissed it as 'intelligent as your alarm clock.
facts.body_md:
During the **1997 match**, Kasparov described Deep Blue as an **"alien opponent"** — something fundamentally different from any human player he had faced. The machine's unexpected moves and lack of visible emotion unsettled him deeply.

After losing, Kasparov reversed course and began dismissing the computer, famously saying it was *"as intelligent as your alarm clock."* Psychologists note this shift as a classic **ego-defense mechanism** — by minimizing the opponent, he could reframe the loss as a fluke rather than a genuine defeat by a thinking machine.

[Deep Blue (chess computer) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Blue_(chess_computer))

facts.title: Grammatical Gender Follows a Pattern
facts.teaser: If a language marks gender in the third person ('he/she'), it always marks it in the second person too.
facts.body_md:
Linguist Joseph Greenberg discovered an **implicational universal**: if a language distinguishes grammatical gender in the third person (like English "he" vs. "she"), it will always also distinguish gender in the **second person** ("you") — though the reverse is not necessarily true.

This pattern holds across unrelated language families worldwide. It suggests that gender systems develop in a predictable order, starting with distinctions closest to the speaker and expanding outward. Languages like Arabic follow this pattern perfectly, with gendered forms of "you" alongside "he/she."
