[Linguistic universal (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_universal)

facts.title: The $100,000 Fredkin Chess Prize
facts.teaser: Edward Fredkin offered $100,000 in 1980 for the first computer to beat a world chess champion — it took 17 years.
facts.body_md:
In **1980**, computer scientist Edward Fredkin established a **$100,000 prize** at Carnegie Mellon University for the first computer program to defeat a reigning world chess champion in a regulation match. At the time, most experts believed it would happen within a decade.

The prize went unclaimed for **17 years** until Deep Blue's victory over Kasparov in 1997. The money was split between the members of the Deep Blue team. Fredkin had also created smaller prizes for intermediate milestones — $5,000 for the first computer to achieve master rating and $10,000 for grandmaster rating.

[Fredkin Prize (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredkin_Prize)

facts.title: AlphaGo Defeated a Go Pro Without Handicap
facts.teaser: In October 2015, AlphaGo became the first program to beat a professional Go player on a full board without handicap.
facts.body_md:
In October **2015**, Google DeepMind's **AlphaGo** defeated European Go champion Fan Hui **5–0** on a full 19×19 board without handicap — the first time any computer program achieved this feat. Go had long been considered far harder for computers than chess due to its vastly larger search space.

Unlike Deep Blue's brute-force approach, AlphaGo used **deep neural networks** trained through self-play and reinforcement learning. The victory was kept secret until published in *Nature* in January 2016, shocking the Go and AI communities simultaneously.

[AlphaGo (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlphaGo)

facts.title: AlphaGo changed how societies talk about AI
facts.teaser: Its win mattered not only technically, but symbolically.
facts.body_md:
When AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in **2016**, the result was discussed as more than a game result. It became a public symbol of changing power in artificial intelligence, education, and industry. Some milestones matter because they shift what entire societies think is coming next.

[AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlphaGo_versus_Lee_Sedol)

facts.title: The Ship of Theseus is still unsolved
facts.teaser: If you replace every plank of a ship, is it still the same ship?
facts.body_md:
The **Ship of Theseus** is a thought experiment from ancient Greece: if you gradually replace **every plank** of a wooden ship, is the resulting vessel the same ship? And if you rebuild the original from the old planks, which one is the "real" ship? After 2,500 years, philosophers still disagree on the answer.

[More on the Ship of Theseus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_of_Theseus)

facts.title: The move AlphaGo never saw coming
facts.teaser: Lee Sedol's famous move 78 in game 4 broke AlphaGo's expectations and led to its only loss against a human.
facts.body_md:
Lee Sedol's move 78 in the fourth AlphaGo match became known as the **"divine move"** because it landed where the system's policy network had assigned almost no probability. AlphaGo suddenly had to search a line it had not prepared for.

That surprise did not make the program useless, but it exposed a real limit of early game-playing AI: when its learned intuition missed a rare idea, the rest of the system could wobble with it. Sedol went on to win the game, the only official AlphaGo defeat against a human player.

[AlphaGo (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlphaGo)

facts.title: A giant ring system hid a star for weeks
facts.teaser: In 2007, J1407b appears to have dimmed its star with a vast ring system that would dwarf Saturn's.
facts.body_md:
Astronomers think the object known as **J1407b** passed in front of its star with an enormous ring system in 2007. The eclipse pattern was so deep and so complex that it looked nothing like a normal planet transit.

The proposed rings would span tens of millions of kilometers, far larger than Saturn's, and may have contained gaps carved by forming moons. Researchers did not realize what they were looking at for years, which made the event even more startling in hindsight.

[J1407b (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J1407b)

facts.title: AlphaGo Zero learned Go in three days
facts.teaser: AlphaGo Zero reached superhuman strength from self-play alone and surpassed earlier AlphaGo systems within days.
facts.body_md:
AlphaGo Zero started with only the rules of Go and improved by playing against itself, without studying human games. After about **three days** of self-play, it had already defeated the earlier AlphaGo version that beat Lee Sedol.

That result mattered because it showed that strong search combined with learning can discover its own patterns instead of copying expert examples. In other words, the system built a powerful Go intuition from mathematics and repetition rather than from human tutoring.

[AlphaGo Zero (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlphaGo_Zero)

facts.title: Ke Jie said AlphaGo rewrote Go
facts.teaser: After losing to AlphaGo, Ke Jie said the machine showed humans had misunderstood strategy for thousands of years.
facts.body_md:
When world champion **Ke Jie** lost to AlphaGo in 2017, he said it felt as if the machine had revealed flaws in human Go tradition. His reaction captured how strange AlphaGo's style looked even to the best players alive.

The remark was not just frustration. AlphaGo often chose moves that first seemed mysterious, then later looked elegant and strong, almost like a new mythology of the game had appeared overnight.

[AlphaGo versus Ke Jie (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlphaGo_versus_Ke_Jie)

facts.title: Go gives brute-force search no chance
facts.teaser: Go is not just "bigger chess". Its branching factor is so huge that naive search collapses almost immediately.
facts.body_md:
In a typical position, Go offers on the order of **hundreds of legal moves**, far more than chess. That makes exhaustive tree search explode so quickly that older computer-chess methods cannot simply be scaled up.

AlphaGo succeeded by combining search with neural networks that guessed which moves and positions were worth attention. The lesson is a useful myth-buster: more computing power alone is not enough when the decision tree grows too fast.

[Go and mathematics (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_and_mathematics)

facts.title: Lee Sedol retired after facing AlphaGo
facts.teaser: Lee Sedol later said AI felt unbeatable, even though he remained the only player to take an official game from AlphaGo.
facts.body_md:
Lee Sedol retired from professional Go in 2019 and said that artificial intelligence had changed the game permanently. His comments were striking because he was also the person who proved AlphaGo was **not completely invincible**.

That contrast makes his story reflective rather than tragic. A human found the system's weakness once, yet still concluded that the wider direction of the game now belonged to machines and to players learning from them.

[Lee Sedol (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Sedol)

facts.title: Bubble sort is older than many languages
facts.teaser: Bubble sort was being formally discussed in the 1950s, long before most modern programming languages existed.
facts.body_md:
Bubble sort is famous today as the example of what **not** to use on large datasets, but it has deep historical roots. Variants of the method were already being analyzed in the 1950s, making it one of the oldest widely taught sorting ideas.

Its staying power comes from simplicity. Even though it is inefficient, the algorithm is easy to visualize, which is why it still survives in classrooms long after better practical sorts took over real software.

[Bubble sort (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubble_sort)

facts.title: Betty Holberton helped teach computers to sort
facts.teaser: ENIAC and UNIVAC pioneer Betty Holberton also co-authored early work on computerized sorting.
facts.body_md:
Betty Holberton is often remembered for programming **ENIAC**, but she also helped shape practical data processing for early commercial machines. In the early UNIVAC era, she co-authored work on sorting large collections of records efficiently.

That mattered because mid-century computers were not just calculators. They were becoming information machines, and sorting payroll, census, and business data was one of the jobs that turned raw hardware into useful technology.

[Betty Holberton (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Holberton)

facts.title: The Sphere survived the Twin Towers
facts.teaser: The sculpture from Austin J. Tobin Plaza was badly damaged on 9/11, but it was not destroyed.
facts.body_md:
Austin J. Tobin Plaza sat between the Twin Towers and held Fritz Koenig's sculpture **The Sphere**. After the September 11 attacks, the plaza was obliterated, yet the battered sculpture was recovered from the debris.

It was later moved to Battery Park, where its scars became part of its meaning. What began as public art for a business complex turned into a historical witness to one of the most documented events of the modern era.

[The Sphere (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sphere)

facts.title: Timsort is younger than Python
facts.teaser: Python existed for more than a decade before Tim Peters designed Timsort for it in 2002.
facts.body_md:
Timsort became famous as the default sorting algorithm in Python and later in Java, but it is surprisingly recent. Tim Peters created it in **2002** by blending ideas from merge sort and insertion sort.

Its clever trick is to exploit runs that are already ordered in real-world data. Instead of treating every list as random chaos, Timsort looks for existing structure and turns that into faster practical performance.

[Timsort (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timsort)

facts.title: Forest fungi can reverse carbon flow
facts.teaser: In mycorrhizal networks, carbon does not always move the same way. The direction can change with the season.
facts.body_md:
Plants linked by **mycorrhizal networks** can exchange carbon through fungi in the soil, but the traffic is not fixed. Studies have found that the direction of transfer can shift with season and life stage.

That means underground networks are less like a one-way pipeline and more like a dynamic trading system. Young seedlings, mature trees, and spring flowers can all become net donors or receivers at different times of year.

[Mycorrhizal network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycorrhizal_network)

facts.title: Bumblebee bats weigh about two grams
facts.teaser: The bumblebee bat is often cited as the world's smallest mammal by mass, and it is lighter than many coins.
facts.body_md:
The **bumblebee bat**, also called Kitti's hog-nosed bat, weighs roughly two grams and can fit easily in a human palm. Its body is tiny, but it still hunts insects on the wing like larger bats do.

Being so small brings trade-offs. The species lives in limestone caves in Thailand and Myanmar, and habitat disturbance can threaten entire local colonies very quickly.

[Bumblebee bat (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bumblebee_bat)

facts.title: Grace Hopper built the first compiler
facts.teaser: Hopper's A-0 system from 1952 showed that computers could translate symbolic instructions into machine-ready code.
facts.body_md:
In 1952, Grace Hopper's **A-0 system** introduced a radical idea: a computer could take symbolic instructions and turn them into executable machine code. That concept became the foundation of the modern compiler.

The breakthrough was cultural as well as technical. Early programmers often had to think in hardware terms, but compilers let humans describe work at a higher level and pushed computers closer to the tools we use today.

[Compiler (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compiler)

facts.title: Dewey's system began as a tiny booklet
facts.teaser: The first Dewey Decimal Classification appeared in 1876 and fit into a short pamphlet rather than a giant manual.
facts.body_md:
When Melvil Dewey published the first **Dewey Decimal Classification**, it was only a few dozen pages long. The idea was simple but powerful: assign subjects to numbers so books could be shelved in a predictable order.

That numbering scheme quietly changed library culture. Once collections grew, a shared system made browsing, cataloging, and borrowing far easier across institutions.

[Dewey Decimal Classification (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewey_Decimal_Classification)

facts.title: Garum gave Roman cooking an umami boost
facts.teaser: Roman garum was rich in glutamates, which helps explain why the fermented sauce was valued so highly.
facts.body_md:
Garum, the fermented fish sauce of ancient Rome, delivered a strong **umami** taste long before scientists identified glutamate. It was made by letting fish and salt break down into a liquid seasoning packed with savory compounds.

Romans used it across social classes, from ordinary cooking to elite banquets. In flavor terms, it played a role surprisingly close to modern fish sauce or soy sauce: small amounts could transform an entire dish.

[Garum (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garum)

facts.title: Null Island marks 0°N, 0°E
facts.teaser: Null Island is a nickname for the point where the equator meets the prime meridian, a place famous in mapping jokes and data errors.
facts.body_md:
"Null Island" is the playful name for coordinates **0°N, 0°E** in the Gulf of Guinea. It is not a real island, but cartographers and programmers use the term because bad location data often collapses to that exact point.

The joke stuck because it reveals something real about digital maps: when software lacks proper geographic information, the world can suddenly snap to a mathematically neat but humanly meaningless place.

[Null Island (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_Island)

facts.title: Quicksort wins by liking the cache
facts.teaser: Quicksort's big practical advantage is often memory behavior: it works in place and touches nearby data efficiently.
facts.body_md:
Quicksort's average-case complexity is **O(n log n)**, but its real-world speed often comes from the hardware underneath. Because it partitions arrays in place, it tends to use memory caches well and avoids the extra copying some other sorts need.

That is a reminder that algorithm performance is not just about asymptotic notation. On modern machines, the pattern of memory access can matter almost as much as the formal count of comparisons.

[Quicksort (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quicksort)

facts.title: Most languages include nasal sounds
facts.teaser: Consonants like m and n are so common that languages without them are rare exceptions.
facts.body_md:
Nasal consonants such as **m**, **n**, and **ng** appear in the overwhelming majority of the world's languages. They are easy to produce because air can flow through the nose while the mouth shapes the sound.

A few languages are famous for lacking ordinary nasal consonants, which makes them linguistically interesting precisely because they are unusual. The pattern is a good reminder that some speech sounds are close to global defaults.

[Nasal consonant (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_consonant)

facts.title: Radix sort can beat n log n
facts.teaser: Radix sort avoids comparison limits by grouping values digit by digit instead of asking which pair is larger.
facts.body_md:
Comparison sorts are bounded by the famous **O(n log n)** lower limit, but radix sort plays a different game. It processes keys digit by digit, so for fixed-width data like integers, it can run in effectively linear time.

That does not make it universally better. Radix sort works best when the data format is friendly, yet it remains a beautiful example of how changing the model of computation can sidestep an apparent barrier.

[Radix sort (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radix_sort)

facts.title: Male seahorses carry the pregnancy
facts.teaser: In seahorses, the male incubates the eggs in a brood pouch and releases the young himself.
facts.body_md:
Seahorses are famous because the **male becomes pregnant** in the practical sense: the female deposits eggs into his brood pouch, and he fertilizes and carries them until birth.

The arrangement flips many human expectations about reproduction, but it still follows the same biological logic of investment and survival. A protected pouch gives developing young a safer start than drifting exposed in open water.

[Seahorse (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seahorse)

facts.title: Diffie-Hellman was patented a year later
facts.teaser: The famous key-exchange method was published in 1976, then patented in the United States in 1977.
facts.body_md:
Diffie and Hellman introduced public key exchange in 1976, and a U.S. patent followed in **1977**. That timing mattered because it placed a foundational cryptographic idea inside the legal world of licensing and intellectual property.

The story also became messier later, when declassified work showed that British intelligence researchers had discovered similar ideas earlier in secret. In cryptography, legal priority and scientific priority do not always line up neatly.

[Diffie-Hellman key exchange (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffie%E2%80%93Hellman_key_exchange)

facts.title: Hellman wanted Merkle on the name
facts.teaser: Martin Hellman later argued that Ralph Merkle deserved equal billing in the name of public-key cryptography's breakthrough.
facts.body_md:
In 2006, Martin Hellman suggested that the protocol often called **Diffie-Hellman** should really be named Diffie-Hellman-Merkle. His point was that Ralph Merkle's work was crucial to the economic and conceptual birth of public-key cryptography.

Names matter in science because they shape who gets remembered, cited, and funded. A short rename proposal can reveal a much bigger question about how credit gets priced in technical history.

[Diffie-Hellman key exchange (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffie%E2%80%93Hellman_key_exchange)

facts.title: Logjam exposed shared internet weak spots
facts.teaser: Logjam showed that many servers reused the same Diffie-Hellman groups, turning one weak setup into a broad ecosystem risk.
facts.body_md:
The 2015 **Logjam** attack was alarming not only because it targeted Diffie-Hellman, but because so much of the internet relied on the same small set of parameter groups. That kind of reuse meant one successful precomputation could threaten many systems at once.

It is a useful reminder that security has an environment as well as a math problem. When too many machines depend on the same defaults, weakness spreads through the whole ecosystem instead of staying local.

[Logjam (computer security) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logjam_(computer_security))

facts.title: Apollo crews practiced moon-walking on walls
facts.teaser: NASA used a reduced-gravity simulator that let Apollo astronauts rehearse Moon-like motion while partly suspended.
facts.body_md:
Before Apollo crews walked on the Moon, NASA trained them with the **Reduced Gravity Walking Simulator**. The setup tilted astronauts sideways and supported part of their weight so their movements would mimic lunar gravity.

Because of that strange arrangement, trainees sometimes looked as if they were walking on walls. It was an ingenious Earthbound trick for rehearsing a world where every step, hop, and stumble would behave differently.

[Reduced Gravity Walking Simulator (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reduced_Gravity_Walking_Simulator)

facts.title: A "quantum-safe" scheme fell fast
facts.teaser: Supersingular isogeny key exchange was designed for a post-quantum future, yet a classical attack broke it in 2022.
facts.body_md:
Supersingular isogeny key exchange, or **SIKE**, was one of the most intriguing post-quantum cryptography candidates because it relied on advanced algebraic structures called isogenies. Then, in 2022, researchers broke it with a surprisingly efficient classical attack.

That was a humbling moment for cryptography. A scheme built to survive future quantum computers turned out to be vulnerable to ordinary present-day mathematics.

[Supersingular isogeny key exchange (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supersingular_isogeny_key_exchange)

facts.title: Too many locks used the same prime
facts.teaser: Much internet traffic once relied on a small pool of Diffie-Hellman groups, which sounds secure until everyone shares the same lock design.
facts.body_md:
For years, huge amounts of encrypted internet traffic relied on just a few standard **1024-bit Diffie-Hellman groups**. That created a myth of diversity: many sites looked independent, yet deep down they often depended on the same mathematical parameters.

If an attacker invested enough effort to precompute one of those shared groups, the payoff could apply far beyond a single target. In security, variety is sometimes less real than it appears.

[Logjam (computer security) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logjam_(computer_security))

facts.title: Y2K was not caused by lazy coding
facts.teaser: Two-digit years were often a deliberate cost-saving choice when memory and storage were painfully expensive.
facts.body_md:
The Y2K bug is often mocked as shortsighted programming, but in the 1960s and 1970s memory and storage were expensive enough that every byte mattered. Using **two-digit years** was often an economic compromise, not pure carelessness.

That choice created a technical debt bill for the future. What looked like a tiny shortcut on one machine eventually became a global maintenance problem once software survived far longer than its creators expected.

[Y2K problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y2K_problem)

facts.title: Bob Bemer warned about Y2K for decades
facts.teaser: Bob Bemer noticed the year-2000 risk in the 1950s and kept warning institutions long before the public panic.
facts.body_md:
Programmer **Bob Bemer** recognized the two-digit year problem as early as 1958 and spent years trying to get major institutions to care. His story is a reminder that technical warnings often arrive decades before anyone budgets to fix them.

There is something reflective in that timeline: a problem can be real, documented, and still ignored simply because it belongs to the future rather than to the current quarter.

[Bob Bemer (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Bemer)

facts.title: Y2K fixes cost hundreds of billions
facts.teaser: Global remediation spending for Y2K is commonly estimated in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
facts.body_md:
By the late 1990s, governments and companies were spending **hundreds of billions of dollars** to inspect code, replace systems, and test date handling before the millennium rollover. Few software bugs have ever produced a cleanup bill on that scale.

The cost bought something hard to see: an anticlimax. Because so much work succeeded quietly, many people later assumed the danger had been exaggerated rather than heavily mitigated.

[Y2K problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y2K_problem)

facts.title: David Eddy coined "Y2K" in 1995
facts.teaser: Programmer David Eddy said the now-universal label came to him quickly after he rejected clumsier alternatives.
facts.body_md:
The label **Y2K** was coined by programmer David Eddy in 1995, giving a short, memorable name to a sprawling technical problem. He later said the phrase came to him almost instantly after he dismissed less elegant options.

Names can influence how fast an idea spreads. A compact term helped turn a niche date-format issue into something engineers, managers, journalists, and the public could all talk about.

[Y2K problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y2K_problem)

facts.title: Korea lost 30 royal portraits in one fire
facts.teaser: A 1954 fire in Busan destroyed 30 official portraits of Korean kings. Many had survived wars, but not that urban blaze.
facts.body_md:
The 1954 Yongdusan fire swept through central Busan and erased a remarkable part of Korea's royal record. Among the losses were **30 state portraits** of Joseon kings, objects used in court ritual as well as remembrance.

Because royal portraits were copied only in limited numbers, each loss mattered. The fire became a reminder that archives can survive centuries of conflict yet still vanish in a single modern disaster.

[1954 Busan Yongdusan fire (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1954_Busan_Yongdusan_fire)

facts.title: Y2K even tripped breathalyzers in Hong Kong
facts.teaser: At the start of 2000, Y2K glitches hit devices in very specific places. Hong Kong breathalyzers and taxi meters in Jiangsu both failed.
facts.body_md:
The Y2K problem was not just a story about giant mainframes. It also disrupted **local hardware in specific regions**, including police breathalyzers in Hong Kong and taxi meters in Jiangsu, China.

Those failures are a good reminder that software bugs travel through geography. The same date rollover could create different practical problems depending on what machines a city relied on.

[Y2K problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y2K_problem)

facts.title: Douglas firs share more carbon with kin
facts.teaser: Douglas firs linked by fungal networks tend to send more carbon to close relatives. The pattern hints at plant kin recognition.
facts.body_md:
In forests, roots and fungi can form **mycorrhizal networks** that move nutrients and chemical signals between plants. Experiments with Douglas firs suggest that more carbon may flow between closely related trees than between distant ones.

Researchers interpret that pattern as a sign that plants are not entirely passive neighbors. Even without brains, they may respond differently to relatives sharing the same underground network.

[Mycorrhizal network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycorrhizal_network)

facts.title: Polar bear fur is transparent
facts.teaser: Polar bears do not have white pigment in their fur. Their hairs are mostly transparent and scatter light.
facts.body_md:
A polar bear's coat looks white, but each hair is largely **transparent and hollow**. The bright appearance comes from the way the fur scatters visible light rather than from white coloring.

That structure helps the animal in Arctic conditions. The fur works with dark skin and thick fat, giving camouflage while supporting heat balance in extreme cold.

[Polar bear (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_bear)

facts.title: Apollo software was woven into memory
facts.teaser: Parts of the Apollo Guidance Computer stored programs in memory woven by hand. The code was literally threaded into hardware.
facts.body_md:
The Apollo Guidance Computer used **core rope memory**, a read-only system in which wires were threaded through or around magnetic cores to encode bits. In effect, software had to be physically woven into the machine.

That made updates slow, but it also made the finished programs durable and compact. The method shows how early space computing solved reliability problems with clever hardware design.

[Core rope memory (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Core_rope_memory)

facts.title: Kabuki stages spun before modern turntables
facts.teaser: Japanese kabuki theaters used revolving stages long before such effects became common in the West. The machinery changed how audiences saw scene changes.
facts.body_md:
Kabuki popularized the **mawari-butai**, a revolving stage introduced in 18th-century Japan. Instead of hiding scene changes behind a curtain, theaters could rotate one setting away and bring another into view.

The trick was more than decoration. It let performances feel fluid and cinematic centuries before film existed, showing how stage technology can reshape culture itself.

[Kabuki (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabuki)

facts.title: Escoffier used umami before it had a name
facts.teaser: Auguste Escoffier built deep savory flavors decades before scientists described umami. His kitchens relied on reductions, stock, and patient layering.
facts.body_md:
French chef Auguste Escoffier created dishes rich in **savory depth** in the late 19th century, even though the word "umami" did not yet exist in Western cooking. He repeatedly concentrated flavor with stocks, meat extracts, and slow reductions.

That makes him a useful bridge between culinary practice and food science. Cooks had already learned how to intensify umami long before chemistry explained why those dishes tasted so full.

[Umami (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami)

facts.title: The oldest Olympic champion won at 64
facts.teaser: Swedish shooter Oscar Swahn won Olympic gold at age 64. Precision sports can reward steadiness more than raw speed.
facts.body_md:
Oscar Swahn became the **oldest Olympic gold medalist** when he won in running deer shooting at the 1912 Stockholm Games. He was 64, an age at which most Olympic careers are long over.

His record survives because some events depend less on sprinting power and more on control, timing, and concentration. It is a reminder that athletic excellence does not always peak young.

[Oscar Swahn (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Swahn)

facts.title: A Y2K bug billed 100 years of late fees
facts.teaser: A video store in South Korea once charged a customer as if a tape were 100 years overdue. Computer errors can feel absurd, but people still react to them emotionally.
facts.body_md:
A South Korean video store's software once calculated a rental as **100 years late**, producing an eye-popping fee of 8 million won. The glitch came from the Y2K date rollover, not from any real human mistake.

Cases like this are memorable because they reveal how strongly people trust printed totals and screens. Even an obviously impossible number can trigger embarrassment, stress, or panic before anyone checks the logic behind it.

[Y2K problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Y2K_problem)

facts.title: Sign languages are not spoken languages on hands
facts.teaser: Sign languages have their own grammar, word order, and idioms. They are full natural languages, not manual copies of speech.
facts.body_md:
American Sign Language, Polish Sign Language, and other signed systems are **independent natural languages**. Their grammar can rely on handshape, motion, facial expression, and use of space rather than on sound.

That is why a signed language is not simply a spoken language transferred into gestures. It develops its own structure, history, and regional variation within Deaf communities.

[Sign language (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sign_language)

facts.title: Exchange hit its own mini Y2K in 2022
facts.teaser: Microsoft Exchange failed on January 1, 2022 because one date value overflowed a signed integer. Mail piled up in queues until a fix arrived.
facts.body_md:
The so-called **Y2K22 bug** struck Microsoft Exchange's malware filtering engine when it tried to parse a date-based version number that no longer fit the expected numeric range. As a result, some servers stopped processing email normally.

It was a very modern reminder of an old lesson: software often hides assumptions about calendars and numbering. When those assumptions break, even routine infrastructure can jam.

[Year 2022 problem (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_2022_problem)

facts.title: House numbers spread for states, not mail
facts.teaser: Early house numbering in Europe was pushed by governments that wanted easier taxation, conscription, and policing. Postal convenience came later.
facts.body_md:
Many cities adopted house numbering because administrations wanted to **count people more efficiently**. Officials could tax households, draft soldiers, and track residents more easily once every building had a stable identifier.

That means a familiar part of urban life began as a tool of state organization. What now feels ordinary was once a visible sign of expanding bureaucracy.

[House numbering (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_numbering)

facts.title: Moore revised his rule in 1975
facts.teaser: Gordon Moore's famous prediction changed over time. In 1975 he slowed the expected doubling pace from one year to roughly two.
facts.body_md:
Moore's original 1965 article predicted annual growth in transistor density, but he later **revised the timetable**. By 1975, he argued that doubling about every two years was a better fit for the industry's trajectory.

That update matters because "Moore's Law" was never a statute carved in stone. It was a moving forecast that engineers and companies kept testing against reality.

[Moore's law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%27s_law)

facts.title: Moore's Law worked partly because firms chased it
facts.teaser: The chip industry treated Moore's Law like a business target, not just an observation. Investment plans were built around keeping pace.
facts.body_md:
Moore's Law is often described as a **self-fulfilling economic roadmap**. Semiconductor companies spent enormous sums on fabrication, design, and research partly because the industry expected steady transistor growth.

In that sense, the forecast helped finance its own future. Once customers, investors, and engineers planned around the curve, falling behind carried real commercial risk.

[Moore's law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%27s_law)

facts.title: Chip fabs got expensive on a brutal curve
facts.teaser: Rock's Law says chip factories become vastly more expensive over time. Progress in computing also has a growing material cost.
facts.body_md:
Rock's Law, sometimes called Moore's second law, says the price of a leading semiconductor fab tends to **double every few years**. Faster chips do not arrive by math alone; they require bigger buildings, cleaner rooms, and more complex tools.

That makes computing progress an environmental story as well as a technical one. Each manufacturing leap depends on more energy, more materials, and more industrial infrastructure.

[Moore's law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%27s_law)

facts.title: A balloon disaster left a hand-holding tomb
facts.teaser: Two victims of the Zénith balloon catastrophe are shown holding hands on their grave monument. The memorial turned an aeronautical tragedy into a lasting image.
facts.body_md:
The 1875 ascent of the **Zénith** became one of the most famous balloon disasters of the 19th century. When the crew climbed to extreme altitude, several men lost consciousness from lack of oxygen.

A memorial to two of the victims depicts them holding hands, giving the accident an unusually intimate afterlife in public memory. It links early flight not just with daring, but with the real risks of exploring the upper atmosphere.

[Zénith (balloon) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C3%A9nith_(balloon))

facts.title: Moore joked his law broke Murphy's Law
facts.teaser: In 2006, Gordon Moore quipped that his law violated Murphy's Law. The joke captured how unusual sustained improvement really was.
facts.body_md:
Moore once joked that **"Moore's law is a violation of Murphy's law"** because things kept getting better instead of worse. Beneath the humor was a real point: exponential improvement over decades is rare and hard to maintain.

The math behind the curve is simple to state but brutal to deliver. Every new generation demanded tighter manufacturing, better design tools, and fewer mistakes across a huge supply chain.

[Moore's law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%27s_law)

facts.title: Chips now hold tens of billions of transistors
facts.teaser: Modern processors passed 90 billion transistors, far beyond the early integrated-circuit era. Numbers that once sounded impossible became ordinary product specs.
facts.body_md:
By the mid-2020s, commercially available processors had climbed beyond **90 billion transistors**. Early integrated circuits began with counts so small that the modern figures feel almost mythical by comparison.

The contrast is one reason Moore's Law became such a cultural symbol. It turned invisible miniaturization into a story of staggering numbers that ordinary people could still grasp.

[Moore's law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%27s_law)

facts.title: People keep declaring Moore's Law dead
facts.teaser: Nvidia's Jensen Huang said Moore's Law was dead, while Intel argued otherwise. The phrase survives partly because no one agrees on exactly what counts as alive.
facts.body_md:
In 2022, Jensen Huang argued that **Moore's Law was dead**, while Pat Gelsinger pushed back. The disagreement was not just about transistor counts, but about whether cost, speed, and practical computing gains were still improving on the old curve.

That is why announcements of its death keep returning. The law is part technical metric, part industry slogan, and part myth about progress.

[Moore's law (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore%27s_law)

facts.title: A transistor once fit in a single atom
facts.teaser: In 2012, researchers at UNSW built a working transistor from a precisely placed phosphorus atom in silicon. Miniaturization reached a scale that once sounded theoretical.
facts.body_md:
Researchers at the University of New South Wales demonstrated a **single-atom transistor** by positioning a phosphorus atom inside a silicon crystal and controlling current through it. It was a striking symbol of how far miniaturization had gone.

The result also raises a reflective question about limits. When devices approach atomic scales, future progress depends less on simple shrinking and more on entirely new ways of engineering computation.

[Single-atom transistor (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-atom_transistor)

facts.title: Dennard scaling gave computers a free speed era
facts.teaser: For years, smaller transistors also meant cooler and faster chips. When Dennard scaling broke down, automatic speed gains largely ended.
facts.body_md:
Dennard scaling predicted that shrinking transistors would keep **power density roughly constant**, allowing chips to run faster without overheating. For a long time, that gave computing a kind of free lunch: each generation often improved speed without demanding major software changes.

Around the mid-2000s, that pattern weakened. Since then, many gains have come from multicore designs, parallelism, and specialized hardware instead of just higher clock rates.

[Denard scaling (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennard_scaling)

facts.title: IBM packed 50 billion transistors into 2 nm
facts.teaser: IBM's 2021 2 nm demonstration squeezed 50 billion transistors onto a chip about fingernail size. Advanced fabrication keeps turning abstract nanometers into usable devices.
facts.body_md:
In 2021, IBM unveiled a **2 nanometer test chip** with about 50 billion transistors on an area roughly the size of a fingernail. The headline number was not just about scale, but about how precisely modern fabrication can place and shape structures.

Announcements like that matter because they preview techniques that later influence real products. They are snapshots of what the next manufacturing era might make practical.

[2 nm process (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_nm_process)

facts.title: Big discoveries often happen more than once
facts.teaser: Historians of science note that important ideas are often discovered independently by several people. The timing of knowledge is not always as individual as legends suggest.
facts.body_md:
Scholars have long pointed out the pattern of **multiple independent discovery**. When the same tools, questions, and methods spread through a period, different researchers can reach similar breakthroughs without copying one another.

That makes the history of science less like a parade of lone geniuses and more like a landscape of shared conditions. Some ideas become "ready" for discovery.

[List of multiple discoveries (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_multiple_discoveries)

facts.title: Null Island is a map error trap
facts.teaser: Null Island is the nickname for the point at 0° latitude and 0° longitude. It became famous because bad datasets keep placing missing coordinates there.
facts.body_md:
Null Island is not a real island but the **imaginary point where the equator meets the prime meridian** in the Gulf of Guinea. Cartographers and programmers joke about it because broken geodata often defaults to 0,0.

That makes it a small lesson in digital geography. Even maps reveal where software assumptions leak into the physical world.

[Null Island (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_Island)

facts.title: Black walnuts chemically bully their neighbors
facts.teaser: Black walnut trees release juglone, a compound that suppresses nearby plants. Some species struggle to grow at all under them.
facts.body_md:
Black walnut trees produce **juglone**, a chemical that can interfere with growth in surrounding plants. Gardeners notice it because tomatoes, apples, and other sensitive species may wilt or fail near the tree.

This is a classic example of allelopathy, in which one plant changes the local biology of another through chemistry. A forest or garden is not just a crowd of neighbors but an active biochemical contest.

[Juglone (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juglone)

facts.title: Frogs often eat their own shed skin
facts.teaser: Many frogs peel off their skin about once a week and swallow it. The behavior helps recycle nutrients and may reduce traces left for predators.
facts.body_md:
Frogs regularly shed the outer layer of skin in a process called **sloughing**. Instead of leaving it behind, many species pull the loosened skin toward the mouth with their legs and eat it.

That habit may help them recover nutrients and keep the skin surface in working order. It also means they leave less obvious biological litter in places where predators could notice them.

[Frog (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frog)

facts.title: The first GMO food sold was a tomato
facts.teaser: The Flavr Savr tomato became the first genetically engineered food approved for sale in the United States. It was designed to soften more slowly after harvest.
facts.body_md:
The **Flavr Savr tomato** reached the U.S. market in the 1990s as the first genetically engineered food approved for human consumption there. Its modification aimed to slow softening so the fruit would hold up better during shipping and storage.

Commercially it did not transform agriculture, but technologically it marked a new stage in crop engineering. It showed that biotechnology could target shelf life, not just yield or pest resistance.

[Flavr Savr (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flavr_Savr)

facts.title: An Osborne looked huge beside an iPhone
facts.teaser: The Osborne Executive portable of 1982 was vastly heavier and larger than a 2007 iPhone, yet far weaker. Personal computing shrank with astonishing speed.
facts.body_md:
The Osborne Executive was marketed as a portable computer in 1982, but by modern standards it was **enormous and expensive**. Compared with an early iPhone, it weighed far more, took up vastly more space, and offered a tiny fraction of the processing power.

The comparison is memorable because it compresses decades of progress into a single object. Personal computing did not just get faster; it became radically smaller, cheaper, and more everyday.

[Osborne Executive (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osborne_Executive)

facts.title: Dashi works because umami compounds team up
facts.teaser: Japanese dashi combines kombu and bonito to create stronger savory taste than either alone. Different umami molecules amplify one another.
facts.body_md:
Dashi is a classic example of **umami synergy**. Kombu contributes glutamate, while bonito flakes add nucleotides such as inosinate, and together they create a stronger savory impression than either ingredient can produce on its own.

That is why some famous food pairings feel almost magically balanced. Good cooking sometimes depends on chemistry hiding inside tradition.

[Umami (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami)

facts.title: The marathon's odd length came from London
facts.teaser: The standard 42.195 km marathon distance comes from the 1908 London Olympics route. A royal start and stadium finish helped lock in the number.
facts.body_md:
The marathon was not always 42.195 kilometers. That now-standard distance traces back to the **1908 London Olympics**, where the course was adjusted so the race could start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box.

Later, the length became official and turned one local arrangement into a global rule. An arbitrary event-day choice ended up defining one of the world's most famous races.

[Marathon (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon)

facts.title: Linux rules the Top500
facts.teaser: Every machine on the Top500 supercomputer list now runs Linux.
facts.body_md:
Linux gradually displaced every rival operating system in high-performance computing. Since 2017, **all Top500 supercomputers** have used Linux.

That dominance comes from flexibility: research teams can tune kernels, drivers, and schedulers for specialized hardware instead of waiting for a closed vendor roadmap.

[Linux (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux)

facts.title: BSL and ASL are not alike
facts.teaser: British and American Sign Language are not mutually intelligible.
facts.body_md:
Despite the shared spoken language background of the UK and US, **British Sign Language** and **American Sign Language** developed along different historical lines.

ASL was shaped in part by French Sign Language, while BSL belongs to a separate sign-language family. Sign languages follow their own histories, not the borders of spoken English.

[British Sign Language (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Sign_Language)

facts.title: When does a thing stay itself?
facts.teaser: The Ship of Theseus asks whether an object stays the same after every part is replaced.
facts.body_md:
The **Ship of Theseus** is a classic puzzle about identity over time. If each plank of a ship is replaced one by one, philosophers ask whether it is still the same ship.

The paradox becomes sharper if someone rebuilds the original planks into a second ship. It is a simple thought experiment with deep consequences for memory, ownership, and personal identity.

[Ship of Theseus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_of_Theseus)

facts.title: Linux powers most big websites
facts.teaser: Linux runs the vast majority of the world's busiest web servers.
facts.body_md:
Linux became the default operating system for internet infrastructure because it is **stable, adaptable, and cheap to deploy** at scale.

That is why it powers most major web servers, from small cloud instances to massive data-center fleets serving millions of users.

[Linux (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux)

facts.title: Innocent until proven guilty
facts.teaser: The presumption of innocence makes the accuser carry the burden of proof.
facts.body_md:
In many legal systems, a defendant must be treated as **innocent until proven guilty**. That principle is meant to protect people from punishment based on rumor, fear, or political pressure.

It also shifts the burden of proof to the prosecution. Courts may differ on details, but the basic idea is that the state must justify its accusation.

[Presumption of innocence (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presumption_of_innocence)

facts.title: Linux grew by fast feedback
facts.teaser: Eric Raymond argued Linux succeeded through quick releases and constant user feedback.
facts.body_md:
Essayist Eric S. Raymond contrasted Linux with software designed by small, closed teams. In his view, Linux advanced through **rapid releases, many contributors, and relentless feedback**.

That model helped bugs surface quickly and let useful ideas spread without waiting for a long formal planning cycle.

[The Cathedral and the Bazaar (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cathedral_and_the_Bazaar)

facts.title: Turing imagined the universal machine
facts.teaser: Alan Turing described a simple abstract machine that became central to computing.
facts.body_md:
In 1936, Alan Turing described an abstract device now called the **Turing machine**. It reads symbols step by step from a tape and follows a fixed set of rules.

The idea mattered because it showed how a very simple machine could represent general computation. Modern computers are built very differently, but the concept still anchors computer science.

[Turing machine (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_machine)

facts.title: The Sun has a tiny neighborhood
facts.teaser: Only a small set of stars and brown dwarfs lie within 20 light-years of the Sun.
facts.body_md:
Our stellar neighborhood is sparse. Within **20 light-years** of the Sun there are only a limited number of known stars, white dwarfs, and brown dwarfs.

That makes nearby objects especially valuable to astronomers: they are close enough for precise measurements of motion, brightness, and in some cases even orbiting planets.

[List of nearest stars and brown dwarfs (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nearest_stars_and_brown_dwarfs)

facts.title: Euclid proved primes never end
facts.teaser: More than 2,000 years ago, Euclid showed there must be infinitely many prime numbers.
facts.body_md:
Euclid's proof is short and elegant. If you multiply a list of known primes and add **1**, the new number cannot divide evenly by any prime in the list.

That means the list was never complete: either the new number is prime itself or it has a prime factor not already included.

[Prime number (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number)

facts.title: Turing never named it that
facts.teaser: The phrase "Turing machine" was popularized by Alonzo Church, not Alan Turing himself.
facts.body_md:
In his 1936 paper, Turing described what he called an **automatic machine**. The now-standard label "Turing machine" was promoted by logician Alonzo Church in later commentary.

It is a reminder that scientific language often settles after the original discovery, once other researchers begin teaching and extending the idea.

[Turing machine (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_machine)

facts.title: Real computers are not infinite
facts.teaser: Strictly speaking, ANSI C is not Turing-complete because real machines have finite memory.
facts.body_md:
People often say a programming language is as powerful as a Turing machine. In practice, **actual computers always run out of memory**, so they never match the ideal mathematical model exactly.

That is why ANSI C is usually treated as "effectively" universal rather than literally identical to a machine with unbounded tape.

[Turing completeness (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_completeness)

facts.title: Tiny rules can create huge searches
facts.teaser: A 3-state Busy Beaver writes just 6 ones, yet larger versions become brutally hard to analyze.
facts.body_md:
The Busy Beaver game asks a deceptively small question: among machines with a fixed number of states, which one does the **most work before halting**?

Even for tiny machines, the search explodes. That is why a toy model with only a few symbols and states still points toward the limits of computation.

[Busy beaver (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busy_beaver)

facts.title: Bitcoin arrived under a pseudonym
facts.teaser: Bitcoin was introduced in 2008 by the still-unidentified Satoshi Nakamoto.
facts.body_md:
The Bitcoin white paper appeared in 2008 under the name **Satoshi Nakamoto**. The identity behind that name remains one of the most famous mysteries in technology.

Nakamoto also mined many early coins and then gradually disappeared from public view, leaving the network to continue without a visible founder.

[Bitcoin (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin)

facts.title: Pizza once cost 10,000 BTC
facts.teaser: The first famous Bitcoin purchase bought two pizzas for 10,000 BTC.
facts.body_md:
In 2010, programmer Laszlo Hanyecz paid **10,000 bitcoins** for two Papa John's pizzas. The deal became a landmark because it showed Bitcoin being used for an ordinary real-world purchase.

Today the event is remembered as Bitcoin Pizza Day, a reminder of how strange early prices can look in hindsight.

[Bitcoin Pizza Day (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_Pizza_Day)

facts.title: Discoveries sometimes happen twice
facts.teaser: Sociologist Robert K. Merton called independent repeated breakthroughs "multiples.
facts.body_md:
Merton used the term **multiples** for cases where different researchers reach similar discoveries independently.

The pattern appears often in the history of science, suggesting that some ideas become reachable once the surrounding tools, data, and questions are in place.

[Multiple discovery (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_discovery)

facts.title: Bitcoin's first block carried a headline
facts.teaser: The Bitcoin genesis block embeds a newspaper line about a bank bailout.
facts.body_md:
The very first Bitcoin block includes the text **"The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks."**

That line served as a timestamp, but many readers also saw it as a political signal about why a decentralized money system might matter.

[Genesis block (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_block)

facts.title: Fungi helped plants reach land
facts.teaser: Mycorrhizal partnerships likely evolved before plants fully colonized land.
facts.body_md:
Mycorrhiza is a partnership between fungi and plant roots. Evidence suggests this relationship is **more than 450 million years old**, dating back to the earliest stages of plant life on land.

Fungi help plants absorb water and minerals, while plants provide sugars. That trade may have made harsh early soils far easier for the first land plants to survive.

[Mycorrhiza (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycorrhiza)

facts.title: Platypuses hunt with electricity
facts.teaser: Platypuses shut their eyes, ears, and nostrils underwater, then hunt by electroreception.
facts.body_md:
When a platypus dives, it closes its **eyes, ears, and nostrils**. That means it cannot rely on sight or hearing while searching for prey.

Instead, receptors in its bill detect tiny electrical signals produced by muscle contractions in worms, shrimp, and other animals moving through the water.

[Platypus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platypus)

facts.title: The first webcam watched coffee
facts.teaser: One of the earliest webcams was built so researchers could check a coffee pot remotely.
facts.body_md:
At the University of Cambridge, researchers pointed a camera at the **Trojan Room coffee pot** so people could see whether any coffee was left before walking over.

It was a tiny practical hack, but it became a famous example of how networked cameras quietly moved from lab convenience into everyday culture.

[Trojan Room coffee pot (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_Room_coffee_pot)

facts.title: Happy Birthday began in class
facts.teaser: The tune of "Happy Birthday to You" started as a classroom song in the 1890s.
facts.body_md:
The melody first appeared as **"Good Morning to All"**, written by the Hill sisters for schoolchildren.

Only later did new birthday lyrics attach themselves to the tune, turning a simple classroom greeting into one of the world's most recognizable songs.

[Happy Birthday to You (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Birthday_to_You)

facts.title: Caffeine is the world's favorite stimulant
facts.teaser: Caffeine is the most widely consumed psychoactive substance on Earth.
facts.body_md:
Caffeine occurs naturally in **coffee, tea, cacao, guarana, and cola plants**. People around the world consume it daily in drinks, desserts, and medicines.

Its effects are mild enough for routine use but strong enough to change alertness, which helps explain its unusual global reach.

[Caffeine (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caffeine)

facts.title: Bitcoin uses real-world electricity
facts.teaser: Bitcoin mining consumes enough electricity to rank with whole countries.
facts.body_md:
Bitcoin relies on proof-of-work, which means miners spend **real energy** solving cryptographic puzzles to secure the network.

That design makes attacks expensive, but it also gives Bitcoin an unusually visible physical footprint for a digital system.

[Bitcoin network (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitcoin_network)

facts.title: Unfinished tasks stick in memory
facts.teaser: The Zeigarnik effect describes why interrupted tasks often stay on your mind.
facts.body_md:
Psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik noticed that people often remember **unfinished activities** better than completed ones.

One explanation is that incomplete tasks leave a kind of mental tension behind. That is why a half-written email or paused project can keep echoing in attention.

[Zeigarnik effect (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeigarnik_effect)

facts.title: ASL is closer to French Sign Language
facts.teaser: American Sign Language is historically closer to French Sign Language than to British Sign Language.
facts.body_md:
American Sign Language did not simply grow out of spoken English in the United States. Its grammar and history were shaped strongly by **French Sign Language** and early Deaf education.

That is why ASL is not especially close to British Sign Language, even though English dominates both countries.

[American Sign Language (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Sign_Language)

facts.title: A satoshi is a tiny fraction
facts.teaser: The smallest Bitcoin unit is one hundred millionth of a coin.
facts.body_md:
A **satoshi** equals 0.00000001 bitcoin. The tiny unit makes it practical to price small payments even if a full bitcoin becomes very expensive.

Its name also keeps the system's mysterious founder embedded in everyday use, since people casually refer to sats without needing whole coins.

[Satoshi (unit) (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoshi_(unit))

facts.title: The Web began at CERN
facts.teaser: Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web to help researchers share documents.
facts.body_md:
Berners-Lee proposed the Web in 1989 while working at CERN. His idea combined **hypertext, internet protocols, and universal addressing** into a system that ordinary people could navigate.

He was not inventing the entire internet, but he built the layer that made it feel browsable and human-scaled.

[World Wide Web (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web)

facts.title: Habeas corpus challenges detention

facts.body_md:
The phrase **habeas corpus** refers to a legal procedure used to challenge unlawful detention. It forces authorities to justify why someone is being kept in custody.

Because of that, it became one of the classic safeguards against arbitrary imprisonment in common-law tradition.

[Habeas corpus (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habeas_corpus)

facts.title: CERN gave the Web away

facts.body_md:
When CERN put the Web into the public domain in 1993, it removed a huge barrier to adoption. Anyone could build servers, browsers, and websites without paying licensing fees.

That decision helped the **World Wide Web** spread from a research tool into a global public platform.

[World Wide Web (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web)

facts.title: Douglas Adams joked about WWW

facts.body_md:
Douglas Adams once joked that **"World Wide Web"** was the only phrase he knew whose abbreviation took longer to say than the original.

The line stuck because it captures an awkward early-web truth: technical convenience and human convenience are not always the same thing.

[World Wide Web (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web)

That is why the nearest stellar neighborhood contains many objects astronomy depends on, even though most people never notice them in the night sky.

facts.body_md: Wydarzenie w Azolli **49 milionów** lat temu – 800 000 lat zakwitów paproci arktycznych – odwróciło globalne ocieplenie poprzez wyciągnięcie CO2 z atmosfery.

facts.teaser: Maksimum termiczne paleocenu i eocenu 55 milionów lat temu zostało zakończone przez rozkwit morza…
facts.body_md: Maksimum termiczne paleocenu i eocenu **55 milionów** lat temu zostało zakończone przez rozkwit morskiego fitoplanktonu, który pochłaniał CO2 z atmosfery.

facts.body_md:

[Środowisko przyrodnicze (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%9Arodowisko_przyrodnicze)

facts.title: Ekstremalne temperatury Merkurego
facts.teaser: W dzień ok. 430°C, w cieniu nawet −180°C—największy dobowy skok temperatury w Układzie Słonecznym.
facts.body_md:
Prawie bez atmosfery **Merkury** nie trzyma ciepła w nocy. W dzień powierzchnia sięga ok. **430°C**, a w zacienionych kraterach spada ku **−180°C**—największy kontrast dzień–noc wśród planet.

[Merkury (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkury)

facts.title: CERN sprawdził promienie kosmiczne i chmury
facts.teaser: Komora CLOUD w CERN wykazała, że promienie kosmiczne same nie tłumaczą współczesnej zmiany klimatu.
facts.body_md:
W eksperymencie **CLOUD** fizycy odtwarzali chemię atmosfery w komorze cząstek CERN. Wyniki pokazały, że **promienie kosmiczne** są zbyt słabe, by wywołać duże zmiany zachmurzenia równoważące ocieplenie cieplarniane.

[Zmienność i zmiana klimatu (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zmienno%C5%9B%C4%87_i_zmiana_klimatu)

facts.title: Nobel 2021 za dynamikę klimatu
facts.teaser: Połowa Nagrody z fizyki poszła za pracę łączącą krótką pogodę z wolnymi zmianami napędzanymi oceanem.
facts.body_md:
**Syukuro Manabe** i **Klaus Hasselmann** dzielili połowę **Nobla z fizyki 2021** za modele pokazujące, jak chaotyczna pogoda uśrednia się w wolniejsze sygnały klimatu—szczególnie przez bezwładność cieplną oceanów.

[Zmienność i zmiana klimatu (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zmienno%C5%9B%C4%87_i_zmiana_klimatu)

facts.title: Zimna nuklearna to prognoza, nie mit
facts.teaser: Modele po wojnie jądrowej przewidują lata ochłodzenia od sadzy—to nie obalone „urban legend”.
facts.body_md:
**Zimna nuklearna** to poważna hipoteza: pożary mogłyby wynieść sadzę w stratosferę, blokując światło i chłodząc powierzchnię latami. **Nie** znaczy to, że każda przeszła wojna już ją wywołała—chodzi o skutek dużej wymiany uderzeń.

[Zmienność i zmiana klimatu (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zmienno%C5%9B%C4%87_i_zmiana_klimatu)

facts.title: Słoje drzew stały się archiwum klimatu
facts.teaser: Dendrochronologia dojrzała jako narzędzie klimatyczne dopiero w latach 60.—z precyzyjnym datowaniem.
facts.body_md:
Porównywanie **słojów** żywych i martwych drzew pozwala datować dawne susze i mrozy. Metoda stała się wiarygodnym **archiwum klimatu** w **latach 60. XX wieku** po długim dopracowaniu technik krzyżowego datowania.

[Zmienność i zmiana klimatu (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zmienno%C5%9B%C4%87_i_zmiana_klimatu)

facts.title: Ląd wysycha w zaskakujący sposób
facts.teaser: Gdy ląd nagrzewa się szybciej niż oceany, wilgotność względna może spadać mimo większej wilgoci bezwzględnej.
facts.body_md:
**Wilgotność względna** nad lądem w wielu regionach maleje, choć **wilgotność bezwzględna** często rośnie. Cieplejszy grunt szybciej ogrzewa powietrze nad kontynentami niż nad oceanami, więc powietrze może pomieścić więcej pary bez wrażenia wilgoci.

[Sprzężenie klimatyczne (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprz%C4%99%C5%BCenie_klimatyczne)

facts.title: Melnick 42 waży ok. 189 razy więcej niż Słońce
facts.teaser: Ten hiperolbrzym w Wielkim Obłoku Magellana należy do najbardziej masywnych zmierzonych gwiazd.
facts.body_md:
**Melnick 42** to świetlista **hiperolbrzymia** w **Wielkim Obłoku Magellana**. Szacunki dają masę ok. **189 razy** większą od Słońca—blisko granicy, powyżej której pojedyncza gwiazda staje się niestabilna.

facts.title: Gdy dwa cyklony tańczą
facts.teaser: Satelity śledzą efekt Fujiwaray—bliskie burze na wspólnej orbicie, aż słabsza słabnie lub znika.
facts.body_md:
Gdy dwa **cyklony tropikalne** zbliżą się na ok. **1400 km**, mogą wejść we wspólną orbitę—**efekt Fujiwaray**. **Satelity** meteorologiczne rejestrują te rzadkie zjawiska; mniejsza burza często traci strukturę i bywa wchłonięta.

[Cyklon tropikalny (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyklon_tropikalny)

facts.title: Dlaczego huragany wirują na odwrót
facts.teaser: Efekt Coriolisa skręca wiatry: na półkuli północnej burze wirują przeciwnie do wskazówek zegara.
facts.body_md:
**Huragany** i tajfuny są na tyle duże, że liczy się obrót Ziemi. Na **półkuli północnej** wirują **przeciwnie do wskazówek zegara**; na południu kierunek się odwraca przez **efekt Coriolisa**.

[Cyklon tropikalny (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyklon_tropikalny)

facts.title: Otwarte okna nie oswoją huraganu
facts.teaser: Szpara w oknach „dla ciśnienia” wpuszcza deszcz i gruz—nie chroni dachu ani ścian.
facts.body_md:
Popularny mit głosi, że trzeba **otworzyć okna**, by huragan nie rozerwał domu. Współczesne budynki i tak nie są szczelne na groźne różnice ciśnień, a otwarte okna **wpuszczają wiatr, deszcz i gruz** bez ochrony dachu czy ścian.

[Cyklon tropikalny (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyklon_tropikalny)

facts.title: Dziesięć głosów ostrzega świat przed cyklonami
facts.teaser: Regionalne centra WMO wydają komunikaty o cyklonach—współpraca, której sto lat temu nie było.
facts.body_md:
Dziś **dziesięć** wyspecjalizowanych centrów uznanych przez **Światową Organizację Meteorologiczną** śledzi cyklony tropikalne basen po basenie. Wymiana prognoz przez granice jest dziś rutyną—choć to stosunkowo młoda warstwa globalnego bezpieczeństwa.

[Cyklon tropikalny (Wikipedia)](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyklon_tropikalny)
